Customize appearance Key Price Levels | OneOption - Stocks & Options Trading Suite Is the safety net going to hold? At this stage we’ve formulated our longer-term market opinion. We’ve determined which stage of the bullish cycle we’re in, we’ve evaluated the price action and we’ve set our measured moves. The market is making higher highs and higher lows. The dips are brief and shallow. Our charts are clean and anything that we add to them is secondary. This is a very important point because we really don’t need anything more than we already have. In the chart below we would enter a long position, add on con�rmation and take gains near the dotted line. Wait for the next dip, enter on support and repeat. Your game plan is to buy dips and to take gains into strength. You might be thinking that there’s no way it could be this easy. I hope this prospect has your heart racing. This is when everything goes to shit for many traders. They add the 100-day moving average to the chart and the SPY touches it. In an instant they �ip from bullish to bearish. They dismiss all of the technicals that suggest a strong up trend. They ignore that the odds of a bounce are much higher than the odds of a breakdown. This time is “different” and they are convinced that a market correction is starting. I can’t explain why this happens, but I see it all of the time. Heed my warning. When you add indicators to a chart they often do more harm than good. Only add what you absolutely need and keep your charts clean. The tools I’m going to describe are self-ful�lling (they work because traders use them). These price levels in�uence behavior. AVWAPQ The green line in the chart below is the anchored volume weighted average price for the quarter (AVWAPQ). I anchor it to Triple Witching (3rd Friday in March, June, September and December) because that is when large trading institutions “roll” their positions. Since this anchor is something that I developed, I don’t believe that other traders use it. AVWAPQ is the performance benchmark for the index since the start of the quarter and I believe that institutional trading algorithms reference it. The end of the quarter is also when Asset Managers are most likely to rebalance for the next quarter. They will start window dressing before the actual end of the quarter because of settlement and they want to spread the order �ow out to reduce market impact when they enter. That’s my theory for placing the anchor at Triple Witching. After observing it for many quarters, I’ve found that price point to be relevant. A friend and fellow trader (Brian Shannon) got me interested in the concept. He wrote a book called Maximum Trading Gains With Anchored VWAP The premise is that Asset Managers use executing brokers like Citadel for large orders. Citadel executes the trade and they honor VWAP over a predetermined time period (it could be days or weeks). The Asset Manager doesn’t have to staff a trade desk and they feel that VWAP is a fair price. AVWAPQ resets every quarter and it will often be the �rst line of support. When the market dips, we want the move to stay fairly tight to the indicator. When it spends very little time below it relative to the time it spends above it, the dip will be brief and shallow. During a strong uptrend, it might only spend a few days below AVWAPQ. As soon as the market closes above it, we have our �rst con�rmation of support and we can buy the dip. We want immediate follow through and we want the market to start distancing itself from AVWAPQ. That would be a sign that buyers are interested. If we don’t get that follow through in a few days, we use a close below AVWAPQ as a stop. That is a fairly tight stop so our losses will be tiny. No harm, no foul. We are in a bullish market cycle and we can evaluate the next AVWAPQ cross. If the move back above it accelerates quickly and the market challenges the recent high from the start of the dip, it’s a sign that buyers are aggressive. That speed is critical because it indicates that buyers see this as an excellent opportunity. Remember, when one side or the other is aggressive, our odds of predicting price movement are high. On a breakout to a new relative high we would add to the position. Look at the chart below and pretend that AVWAPQ doesn’t exist. Focus on the market cycle, the price action and the measured moves. The market is making higher lows and higher highs. It is in an up trend and that is our primary observation. That move lower is just probing for support and that level is more likely to hold than it is to fail. How do I know that? Because the market is in an uptrend! Never lose sight of that. Buy when the market crosses back above AVWAPQ and watch for immediate follow through. Moving Averages For purposes of this course, I will use the term moving average (MA) instead of simple moving average. If I am referencing an exponential moving average I will use EMA and I don’t use it for long-term market analysis. Let’s discuss a major concept �rst. When the 50-day MA crosses the 200-day MA, a new market cycle begins. There’s nothing magical about these crosses, we are simply comparing the short-term price action to the long-term price action. When it is improving we are bullish and when it is deteriorating we are bearish. Golden Cross – The 50-day MA has closed above the 200-day MA. This marks the beginning of a bullish market cycle. Death Cross – The 50-day MA has closed below the 200-day MA. This marks the beginning of a bearish market cycle. The only thing signi�cant about the 50-day, 100-day or 200-day MA is that other traders have them on their daily charts. I don’t use these moving averages for any other time frame. The 200-day moving average is more signi�cant than the 100-day moving average and it is more signi�cant than the 50-day moving average. When AVWAPQ is greater than the 50-day MA and it is greater than the 100-day MA and it is greater than the 200-day MA, the SPY is in a strong up trend. They are all in alignment and you can see that in the chart below. Anything other than this order is less than ideal and our odds of predicting price movement is not as high. It doesn’t mean that we don’t trade, it means that we are more cautious. At the very beginning of the chart below, you can see how the MAs were all converging in the same area. Then they all started to fall into order. That con�rms that the bullish trend is underway. In the far left of the chart, please �nd the 50-day MA (light purple) and the 200-day MA (black). When the 50-day MA is above the 200-day MA the bullish market cycle begins. This is an important point. As traders we want to stay �exible, but this is the exception. Getting the market right on a longer-term basis is the single most important puzzle piece to our trading success. We have a very simple and unambiguous rule base. If we are in a bullish market cycle, our only thought is to buy dips and to add if the price action indicates aggressive buying. When the momentum slows and we approach a measured move, we will start taking gains. Once we’re in back in cash, the price action around the moving averages is going to tell us if it is time to buy. Is that support level (“safety net”) going to hold? When the market tests the 50-day MA, we want it to �y right off of it. If the market doesn’t do that, it is a sign that the selling pressure is a bit heavy. When it spends more time below the 50-day MA, it is likely to test the 100-day MA. When it does so, we want the market to �y off of the 100-day MA before it even touches it. Any cross back above the 50- day MA signals that the dip is over and that it is time to buy. If the market drops below the 100-day and it can’t rally above it quickly, it is likely to test the 200-day MA. This is a very long-term moving average. The market will rarely touch the 200-day MA during a strong up trend and any drop down to it has to be brief (one week). This is likely to be a great buying opportunity and we want the market to start blowing through all of the other moving averages with gusto. When it does so we buy and add on each successive close above another moving average. The market cycle is bullish and our only thought is to buy. The deeper the market probes for support, the better. In the chart below, look at the price action after it tests the 100 and 200-day MAs. These snap back rallies are what we want to catch and these are very high odds windows of opportunity. Look at how tight the price action is after these lows. This is what we dream of. During deep probes, we never entertain the thought of shorting. We are mentally tough. The cycle is bullish and dips are buying opportunities. Trendlines Trendlines are perhaps the oldest form of technical analysis. Any trader with a straight edge can draw them and they are easy to spot visually. Trading programs draw them using algorithms and they know where the major ones are. If you want to take a deep dive into trendlines, read the next article. If not, here are the basics. To draw them, use a log normal chart setting. Connect two highs (or lows) that stand out on the chart. The line should not penetrate the body of any candle and the angle should be no more than 45 degrees. We can draw through wicks and tails, to capture more “touches”. Trendlines take a long time to draw manually, but in this section we are only referencing the longer-term chart of SPY so it won’t take more than a few minutes a week. If the trendline is connecting the highs (H) and it is downward sloping (-), we call that a H-. If the trendline is connecting the highs (H) and it is upward sloping (+), we call that a H+. If the trendline is upward sloping (+) and it is connecting the lows (L), we call it a L+ and if it is downward sloping (-) and it is connecting the lows (L), we call it a L-. Older trendlines that span many months are more relevant than trendlines that span a few weeks. My software automatically draws trendlines. In the chart below I used a setting that allows us to see how they were drawn in the past. Normally, we only look at current trendlines that are “in range”. There might only be one or two of them and this keeps our charts clean. When the bullish cycle is just starting, there will be many breaches above H- trendlines. We want to see nice long green candles through these price points. That will serve as con�rmation that the trend is strong. We can use these breakouts and add to positions, especially if that coincides with a breakout above a major moving average. As the trend matures, we will see more H+ trendlines drawn. They will tell us where we can expect resistance. If the market blows through these levels, we can add to bullish positions. If the market struggles to get through these price points, we have to watch for tiny bodied mixed candles on light volume. That would be a sign that resistance is building and we should be in pro�t taking mode. We also want to note if these H+ trendlines are coinciding with measure moves. In the chart below you can see past “balanced” trendlines and I �nd them to be very reliable. The start and the end point are at least six months apart so they are longer-term trendlines. The distance between the starting point, the end point and the intercept have nice spacing (balanced). These breakouts served as con�rmation and we can add to bullish positions on follow through. If we are going to clutter our charts with indicators, they had better be useful. We never lose sight of the market cycle we are in, the price action and the measured moves. Our mindset during a bullish cycle is to buy dips. AVWAPQ is often the �rst line of support and I believe that trading programs reference it. If the market tests this level and it bounces off of it, we can buy that dip. We want to see immediate follow through and if we get it, we can add to the position. If the market �ounders around a support level without any “lift”, it is likely to drop to the next level of support. We let this “soft patch” run its course. It can test as many support levels as it needs to and we will not entertain shorting. We know that this drop is ultimately going to produce an excellent entry point for bullish trades and we don’t want to miss it. If the 200-day MA is tested, the market won’t spend much time there. This deep probe is likely to attract large buyers (Asset Managers) and the rebound is going to be swift and strong. As the market works its way above the other moving averages, we can add. The faster we move back above these moving averages, the better. That is the sense of urgency we are looking for. If all of the moving averages are in order (AVWAPQ > 50 > 100 > 200), the trend is very strong.

# Analysis of SPY Daily Chart — "Key Price Levels" Chapter

## 1. WHAT IS SHOWN

This is a **daily (D1) candlestick chart of SPY (SPDR S&P 500 ETF)** spanning approximately from **October 2022 through December 2024** — roughly a two-year-plus period. The current price shown is **594.78** in the upper right corner.

The chart displays a major **bullish cycle** that began in late 2022, with the price rising from roughly the 350 area to nearly 600. The overall structure shows a sustained uptrend characterized by a series of higher highs and higher lows, with periodic dips/pullbacks that get bought up.

Four moving averages are overlaid, along with a volume panel at the bottom. Several key annotations highlight the bullish cycle structure, measured move projections, and a higher-low/double-bottom formation.

---

## 2. ANNOTATIONS INVENTORY (Exhaustive)

### **Text Labels & Callouts:**

1. **"SPY - D1"** — Upper left corner, white text. Identifies the instrument and timeframe.

2. **"594.78"** — Upper right area, showing the current/last price level.

3. **"Bullish cycle begins"** — Left side of chart, with a **blue diagonal arrow** pointing down-right toward the price action around **October–November 2022**, approximately in the 350–370 range. This marks the inception point of the entire bull run.

4. **"Higher low double bottom"** — Lower-left portion of the chart, with a **blue arrow** pointing to two troughs that formed around **December 2022 to early January 2023**, approximately in the 375–380 range. The arrow curves downward to the price lows, indicating a classic higher-low/double-bottom reversal pattern that confirmed the bullish cycle.

5. **"Measured moves calculated from this peak to the trough of upcoming dip"** — Left-center area, white text with a line pointing toward a peak around **February 2023** (~415–420 area). This explains the methodology: you take the distance from a prior peak down to the next dip's trough and project that distance upward to estimate the next target.

6. **Moving Average Legend (lower right of price panel):**
   - **"Black = 200-day"** — The black line, the slowest moving average, serving as the major long-term trend indicator
   - **"Blue = 100-day"** — The blue line, intermediate-term trend
   - **"Purple = 50-day"** — The purple/violet line, shorter-term trend
   - **"Green = AVWAPQ"** — The green line, which is the **Anchored VWAP Quarterly** — a volume-weighted average price anchored to the start of each quarter

### **Drawn Lines & Zones:**

7. **Dashed blue horizontal/slightly ascending lines (measured move projections):** There are **three distinct sets of dashed blue lines** visible on the chart:

   - **First dashed line** — Extends from roughly the early 2023 area (~415–420) horizontally to the right, projecting a target zone around the **460–470 level**. This corresponds to a measured move from the Feb 2023 peak through the next dip.
   
   - **Second dashed line** — Located in the **480–500 area**, extending from roughly mid-2024, representing another measured move projection from a subsequent peak-to-trough calculation.
   
   - **Third dashed line (highest)** — Located at the top of the chart around the **590–610 area**, representing the most recent measured move projection. The price has reached and is testing this zone at the chart's right edge.

8. **Light purple/lavender shaded vertical columns:** There appear to be **approximately 4–5 shaded vertical zones** at various points along the chart. These appear to highlight significant **consolidation or breakout zones** — periods where price paused, consolidated, and then launched to higher levels. They seem to coincide with areas where the measured move projections were calculated or achieved.

9. **Moving Average Lines (overlaid on price):**
   - **Black (200-day MA):** The slowest, smoothest line. It turns from flat/declining to rising around early-mid 2023 and has remained in a steady upward slope since. Price has stayed consistently above it for the majority of the bull run.
   - **Blue (100-day MA):** Tracks closer to price than the 200-day. It turned up earlier and has served as support on several pullbacks.
   - **Purple (50-day MA):** The most reactive to price, closest to the candles. It has acted as the first line of dynamic support during shallow pullbacks.
   - **Green (AVWAPQ):** The quarterly anchored VWAP weaves through price action, resetting each quarter. It tends to track near the 50-day MA and provides context for institutional positioning relative to the quarter's average price.

10. **Volume panel (bottom):** Shows red and blue/green volume bars. Notable volume spikes appear at key turning points — particularly around the October 2022 lows, during breakout periods (corresponding to the shaded zones), and during some of the pullbacks.

---

## 3. PATTERN OR CONCEPT BEING TAUGHT

### **Primary Concept: Bullish Market Cycle Structure & Measured Moves as Key Price Levels**

This chart teaches traders how to identify and navigate a **long-term bullish cycle** using:

#### **A. Bullish Cycle Identification:**
- The cycle begins with a **higher low / double bottom** formation (Oct–Dec 2022) — a failed attempt to make new lows that signals a shift from bearish to bullish sentiment.
- Confirmation comes when price breaks above prior resistance and the moving averages begin to stack bullishly (50-day above 100-day above 200-day).

#### **B. Measured Move Projections:**
The core technique taught is:

> **"When price forms a peak and then pulls back to a trough (dip), measure that distance (peak-to-trough). Project that same distance upward from the peak to estimate the next price target/key level."**

This creates upside **price targets** that serve as key resistance/profit-taking levels. The chart shows this methodology applied **multiple times** throughout the bull cycle, with each successive measured move projection being reached and often exceeded.

#### **C. Moving Average Confluence as Support:**
The rule here is:

> **"When price is above all major moving averages (50, 100, 200-day) and they are stacked in bullish order (50 > 100 > 200), the trend is firmly bullish. Pullbacks to these moving averages — especially the 50-day and 100-day — represent buying

Customize appearance Price Action - Applying Our Lessons - Part 1 | OneOption - Stocks & Options Trading Suite Price Action – Applying Our Lessons – Part 1 Market First 9 min read 2025-01-28 Let’s conduct longer-term technical analysis for the market using price action. We will go through an entire year and this is the �rst of four parts. The principles for reading price action can be used for any time frame. If you are a day trader, you would use �ve-minute charts. If you are an investor, you would use weekly charts. My longer-term swing trades last from 3-4 weeks so I will use daily charts to read the price action in this section. Later in the course we will use shorter time frames for overnight swing trades and for day trades. Before we get started I want to mention a few things. The same chart will be posted throughout this article. The longer term chart allows us to see how the current price action �ts into the longer term picture (we call this context). I posted the same chart many times so that you do not have to keep scrolling back in the article to see the data point I am referencing. In the chart you will see hollow candles. These are key bars and they have long bodied candles, short tails/wicks and above average volume. As you know from the previous articles, these candles are very important to us. Finally, we are not using any other forms technical analysis (trendlines or moving averages). This section is purely reading price action. We will add those other forms of technical analysis when we apply everything we’ve learned. 1. The long red candle should be bearish, but notice how we had a long red candle the day before that. When this second long red candle formed, the market gapped higher and all of the losses from the prior day were erased on the open. Eventually, the second red candle did close below the prior red candle. While this price action appears bearish (two long red candles in a row), the overlap tells us that this is not a strong move. Why? If sellers were truly aggressive, the second red candle would never have gapped up the following day. They would have kept the pressure on. This buying pressure is con�rmed the next day when the green bar (hollow) closes above the midpoint of the second red candle. We want those midpoints on these key bars preserved. These are long bodied, mixed candles and they suggest volatility. 2. The market rallied off of the recent low and the long green candle is encouraging. It closed just below horizontal resistance on the daily chart. Unfortunately, it was erased the next day by a long red candle and the midpoint of the green candle was breached (bearish). The interpretation of these two candles and the context from the start of the chart is that conditions are very volatile and there is not a clear sense of market direction. I would not be taking longer term swing trades in this environment because the market could go either way and a big move could be pending. 3. The market is compressing at horizontal resistance and it made a marginal new high (barely got through the old high). The price action before the compression included a bullish hammer and stacked green candles with little to no overlap. This would normally be bullish, but notice how the rally took place on very light volume. The market was not able to advance after making the new high and the tiny bodied candles suggested that sellers were nearby. Why? If buyers were truly aggressive, they would have been able to add to the breakout after those stacked green candles and the volume would have been heavy. 4. This long red candle is con�rmation that we needed to remain cautious. To that point, we have mixed long candles and extreme volatility. The light volume rally to the new high could not be trusted and now it looks like sellers are going to take a turn. The long red candle breached the halfway point of the prior long green candle, it broke horizontal support at the bottom of the compression (shaded blue) and the red candle closed on its low. From a longer term swing viewpoint, it is still too early to take short positions. The recent volatility tells us that the long red candle could quickly be erased. It did come on heavy volume and that gives it more legitimacy. We want to see that midpoint preserved for a few days. If the SPY can’t rally above that midpoint, we might have a shorting opportunity. 5. The midpoint of the long red candle held for a few days and we could have taken bearish swing positions when we had con�rmation that sellers were in control. There was some overlap in the candles on the way down, but the volume was very heavy and there were not any green candles. The long bullish hammer was the �rst sign of support. The low from the bullish hammer held and subsequent candles had tails. Sellers remained aggressive, but the fact that the candles could not close on the low of the day indicated that buyers were interested and that support was forming (tails under body). We can also see mixed, overlapping candles and that tells us that the momentum is starting to wane. From a longer term swing trading standpoint, this is a time to take gains on short positions. Given the magnitude of the drop, the heavy volume and the lower highs, it would be too early to take long swing positions. This is a time to evaluate. 6. The market is trying to bounce after a big drop, but the level of conviction is low. We know that from the light volume. The relative high at this price level retreated instantly/signi�cantly and buyers attempted a breakout a second time. The third attempt failed quickly. The bearish hammer was formed by a gap down. During the day the market tried to rally above the resistance level and we know that from the long wick. Sellers did not squander this opportunity and they pounded the market down, forming the bearish hammer. The next day a long red candle was formed and we saw follow through selling. 7. Conditions remain volatile and the price action from the start of the chart has been all over the board. We can see that a negative bias is starting to form. The market is making lower highs. As long as the midpoint of the long red candle is preserved for a few days, we can take short swing positions. 8. The bottom fell out of the market and it gapped down to a new low for the year. The opening price that day was also the low that day and this giant candle closed on its high. That was a sign of major support. Buyers gobbled up stocks and that candle closed above the midpoint of the previous red candle. This is a very signi�cant intraday reversal because it took place on heavy volume. Swing traders needed to take gains on shorts and a bounce is likely. It is too early to buy from a swing trading standpoint. This is a horizontal support level, but the bias has been to the downside. As I mentioned in the previous article, we need additional con�rmation that support is in after big drops. It would be foolish to think that the market is going to rally and never look back after the selling we have witnessed the last few months. 9. The market has breached the midpoint of the long green candle from the low of the year and sellers continue to probe for support. Notice in the chart that the volume during this probe has been light (blue line < 0). That tells us that sellers are not as aggressive. Also notice that we are �nding support above the low of the year. This is a sign that buyers are defending that support and that they do not believe they will have a chance to buy at that level. The hollow candles in the chart are important since they have long bodies, short tails/wicks and relatively heavy volume. I will post the same chart many times so that the points are easier to reference. 23. In the previous chart we suspected that a light volume bounce might be running out of steam. We are in a bear market so we need to favor the short side. The gap down in the third candle on the chart was the clue and now we want to see that gap hold for a few days. That would be a sign that buyers do not have the power to �ll it. Our suspicions were con�rmed by the long red candle. In the �rst candle with the blue arrow everything looks great. We had that �rst long red candle (23.) and then a doji below the low of that candle and then this long red candle. Everything is going great for a short position. However, notice how the next day the market gapped higher (solid red candle). Sellers regained control and the candle closed on its low, but there were some signs of buying. Also notice now the third candle with the arrow was red, but it had a massive gap up and then it spend the day drifting lower. It closed near its low, but buyers are interested. How do we know? If there were no interest on the part of buyers we would not have gapped higher. Orders to sell would have been layered above the close the previous day and there would not have been a gap up. Swing traders should take some gains here. A bounce looks likely. 25. The market staged a nice little rally and there were a few nice long green candles. ## 1. WHAT IS SHOWN

This is a **daily candlestick chart (D1)** of **SPY** (S&P 500 ETF), covering approximately **mid-August through mid-November 2022**. The chart includes a **volume histogram** at the bottom. The price range spans roughly from ~$348 to ~$430. The overall structure shows a **bear market decline** from the upper-left (~$430) down to a low near ~$348, followed by a significant bounce/rally back toward ~$398.

The chart is the continuation of a price action case study (Part 3), picking up from where previous lessons left off (starting at annotation 23 and continuing through 30). This is an educational chart designed to walk through real-time decision-making in a bear market context.

1. **"23."** — Located in the upper-left area, with a **blue dashed horizontal line** extending to the right. It marks the **mid-point of a prior long red candle** around the ~$413-$415 level. 2. **"24."** — Located on the left side, lower area (~$388-$390), with **three blue upward-pointing arrows** on consecutive candles pointing upward. These arrows mark a sequence where the first long red candle held and buyers stepped in. The arrows indicate continued buying/selling interest at the mid-point of the long red candle. There's a cluster of candles here where the market initially bounced but then reversed.

3. **"25."** — With a **blue dashed horizontal line** extending to the right at approximately the ~$398-$400 level. This marks the **mid-point of the long red candle (23)** that was preserved as resistance. The text describes how the market staged a "nice little rally" with green candles, but the mid-point of candle 23 was preserved. The long red candle (25) erased three prior green candles — very damaging for bulls.

4. **"26."** — With a **blue dashed horizontal line** extending to the right at approximately ~$385 level. This marks where a **long red candle closed on its low on heavy volume**, confirming the short position. The mid-point was preserved and this validated the bearish thesis.

The text notes to watch the sidelines — if the bounce stalls and tiny-bodied candles appear with light volume, another wave of selling could come. Market First 3 min read 2025-01-28 Breakouts can look very convincing, but time will tell the true nature of the move. Here’s what to look for. Below are my actual comments before the open on November 10, 2022. The market had a breakout above a downward sloping trendline, above the 100-day MA and above a horizontal resistance level. This was a reaction to a “lighter than expected” CPI and the breakout came on heavy volume. The market has been in a longer term bearish trend. That context is very important because the move could have been caused by short covering. Why do we care if it was short covering? Short-term traders do not have staying power. They are in and out of positions and they are trying to capture short-term moves. If this was short covering, the breakout could easily fail as that buying dries up. For a sustained move higher we want long term buyers. If Asset Managers feel that the market will be trading higher than this level a year from now, they will start to scale in on the notion that seasonal strength with fuel a year-end rally. Under-allocated Asset Managers will get nervous that they missed a nice entry point and they will buy this breakout. How will we know if Asset Managers are buying? After a nice breakout through multiple resistance levels we will see small dips and increasing volume on rallies. The mid-point of the long green November 10 candle could be tested, but that retest will be gobbled up immediately. Then we will see follow through buying on good volume and the bounce will have follow through immediately (2-3 days). Why does the follow through have to happen immediately? It is a sign that buyers are aggressive. They do NOT believe they will have a better opportunity to enter and they do NOT want to miss this entry point. They will layer bids at lower levels, but when they are not �lled they will start to raise the bid. That process fuels the move higher and the feeding frenzy is on. What happens if we do not see follow through buying and the volume dries up? If the market can’t add to the gains it will be a sign that the November 10 breakout was just a short covering bounce to squeeze short term traders (this includes trading institutions). It would be a sign that Asset Managers are NOT aggressive and that they do NOT feel like this is the last chance to buy stocks at this level. Traders will recognize that there is no follow through and that the volume is light. They will recognize this as a short covering bounce and they will get more aggressive with their shorts. What you read above was actual commentary I provided on November 10th. I just wanted to give you a look at the thought process we were going through at the time. Notice how I framed the context of what had been happening and the price action we were watching for. We did not see follow through buying. Instead we had tight ranges on light volume. This told us that Asset Managers were not buying aggressively and that the chance for follow through was unlikely. The breakout was likely just short covering and traders/institutions will get more aggressive trading from the short side. The market did make a few attempts to move higher, but they were quickly smacked down. The chart below is how everything played out. Not all breakouts are real. th th Given this information, here is our trading game plan on November 17th.

# Detailed Chart Analysis: "Is This Breakout Real or Fake?"

## 1. WHAT IS SHOWN

This is a **daily candlestick chart (D1)** of **SPY (S&P 500 ETF)** covering approximately August 12 through November 7, 2022. The chart displays a clear **longer-term bearish trend** characterized by a series of lower highs and lower lows from August through mid-October, followed by a sharp breakout candle in early November (the November 10th CPI reaction candle). A volume histogram is displayed at the bottom of the chart. Several moving averages and technical overlays are visible, including what appears to be a 100-day moving average (pink line), a shorter-term moving average (black line), and a downward-sloping trendline (blue diagonal line).

The price range spans roughly from ~$348 at the lows to ~$430 at the highs (August), with the breakout candle pushing price to approximately $395.45 (shown on the right axis).

---

## 2. ANNOTATIONS INVENTORY

### **a. "SPY - D1" (Top center, green text)**
- Identifies the instrument (SPY) and timeframe (Daily).

### **b. "ASS: 378.18" (Top left, red text)**
- Appears to be a moving average or indicator value reference point.

### **c. "Is this move real? How will we know and when will we know?" (Upper right area, magenta/pink text)**
- This is the central question being posed to the reader. It sits above the breakout candle area, framing the educational purpose of the chart. It's asking the trader to think critically about whether the breakout is genuine or just a short-covering bounce.

### **d. "Breakout" (Center-right area, green text with a blue arrow pointing down)**
- A blue downward-pointing arrow marks the specific breakout candle — the large green candle on approximately November 10th. This candle broke above:
  - The downward-sloping blue trendline
  - A horizontal resistance/dashed line around the $388-390 level (the 100-day MA zone and horizontal resistance)
- The arrow points directly to the breakout candle to identify the exact moment of the breakout.

### **e. "Heavy volume" (Lower right area, green text with a blue arrow pointing down)**
- A blue arrow points to the volume bar on the day of the breakout, which is significantly taller than surrounding volume bars. This confirms the breakout occurred on notably heavy volume — which the article contextualizes as potentially being short-covering volume rather than genuine institutional buying.

### **f. Blue diagonal trendline (downward-sloping)**
- Drawn from approximately mid-August highs, connecting the series of lower highs. This represents the **downward-sloping trendline** mentioned in the article text. The breakout candle pierces through this trendline.

### **g. Horizontal dashed line (~$388-390)**
- A horizontal dashed blue/cyan line sits around the $388-390 level. This represents the **horizontal resistance level** — likely the convergence of the 100-day moving average and a price-based resistance zone. The breakout candle closed above this level.

### **h. Pink moving average line (likely 100-day MA)**
- A pink/magenta curved line descending from the upper left. This is likely the **100-day moving average** referenced in the article. By November, it's trending downward around the $388-390 area, adding to the resistance cluster.

### **i. Black moving average line (shorter-term)**
- A black line that has been trending below price during the bearish move, appearing to be a shorter-term moving average (possibly 20 or 50-day).

### **j. Post-breakout candles (November 7+ area)**
- After the large green breakout candle, there are a few subsequent candles visible that appear to show the market struggling to follow through — small-bodied candles hovering near the breakout level, which is critically important to the lesson.

### **k. Volume histogram (bottom panel)**
- Shows daily volume bars. Most bars are relatively moderate, but the breakout day's volume bar stands out dramatically, confirming the "heavy volume" annotation.

### **l. "www.oneoption.com" watermark (lower center area, yellow/olive text)**
- Source attribution for the chart.

---

## 3. PATTERN OR CONCEPT BEING TAUGHT

### **Concept: Distinguishing Real Breakouts from Fake Breakouts (Short-Covering Bounces)**

This chart illustrates the critical skill of **evaluating breakout authenticity** by looking at what happens AFTER the breakout rather than being seduced by the breakout itself.

### **The Setup:**
- SPY was in a **sustained downtrend** (bearish trend) with a clear downward-sloping trendline, price below major moving averages, and a series of lower lows/lower highs.
- On November 10, 2022, a "lighter than expected" CPI report triggered a massive rally that broke above:
  1. The downward-sloping trendline
  2. The 100-day moving average
  3. A horizontal resistance level (~$388-390)
- The breakout occurred on **heavy volume**

### **The Rules:**

**Rule 1 — Context Matters:**
"When a breakout occurs within a longer-term bearish trend, be skeptical — the move could be driven by short covering rather than genuine institutional buying."

**Rule 2 — How to Confirm a Real Breakout:**
"When Asset Managers are buying aggressively, you will see:
- Small dips followed by quick recoveries
- Increasing volume on rallies
- The mid-point of the breakout candle may be tested, but it gets immediately bought up
- Follow-through buying within 2-3 days on good volume"

**Rule 3 — How to Identify a Fake Breakout:**
"When the market cannot add to gains after a breakout, when volume dries up, and when there is no follow-through buying within 2-3 days, the breakout was likely a short-covering bounce — and traders/institutions will get MORE aggressive on the short side."

**Rule 4 — The Behavioral Dynamic:**
"Short-term traders create breakouts through short covering but have no staying power. For a sustained move higher, you need long-term buyers (Asset Managers) to step in. Their absence is confirmed by lack of follow-through."

---

## 4. CORE UNDERSTANDING AND NUANCE

### **The Deep Insight:**

The most important lesson here is that **a breakout is not a signal — it is a question**. The breakout itself, no matter how dramatic, tells you very little. What matters is **what happens next**.

"When Asset Managers are buying aggressively, you will see:
- Small dips followed by quick recoveries
- Increasing volume on rallies
- The mid-point of the breakout candle may be tested, but it gets immediately bought up
- Follow-through buying within 2-3 days on good volume"

**Rule 3 — How to Identify a Fake Breakout:**
"When the market cannot add to gains after a breakout, when volume dries up, and when there is no follow-through buying within 2-3 days, the breakout was likely a short-covering bounce — and traders/institutions will get MORE aggressive on the short side."

"Short-term traders create breakouts through short covering but have no staying power. For a sustained move higher, you need long-term buyers (Asset Managers) to step in. Their absence is confirmed by lack of follow-through."

---

## 4. CORE UNDERSTANDING AND NUANCE

### **The Deep Insight:**

The most important lesson here is that **a breakout is not a signal — it is a question**. The breakout itself, no matter how dramatic, tells you very little. What matters is **what happens next**.

Customize appearance Price Action - Putting It All Together | OneOption - Stocks & Options Trading Suite Price Action – Putting It All Together Market First 6 min read 2025-01-28 The longer term price action set the tone for this trading day. By now you know my mantra… market �rst, market �rst, market �rst. That is the starting point for every trade and that is why this lesson is at the beginning of the course. This can be used for stocks as well, but it is critical that you get your market bearings each day before you trade stock. Context is critically important when you are reading price action. What do the longer term daily charts look like? Is the market in a strong trend? Is the market trapped in a trading range longer term? Did we get to the current price with a Lamborghini or a bicycle? Are the candles mixed (weak trend) or are they of a single color (strong trend)? Is there overlap with other candles (weak trend) or are they stacked (strong trend)? All of these questions need to be answered so let’s start with a longer term chart of the SPY and then let’s drill down to an M15 chart and �nally an M5 chart. You can see my comments in the charts below. By the way, all of these comments were posted live in the chat room during the last week so I am not playing “Monday morning Quarterback”. Reading price action is a skill that can be learned and it works. Below the charts you can read the scenarios I am expecting today with the probability of each. At the very bottom I conclude this section with a chart of what happened and a live video that I recorded on the opening bell where I described the price action bar-by-bar. Today the SPY is going to challenge a resistance level at $380 and it will open above it. Stacked green candles with little to no overlap in the �rst 30 minutes would be a sign of heavy buying. That scenario is unlikely because we know that sellers are present based on the recent price action. If we get that pattern the SPY will start to �ll in the D1 gap and we could have a few more days of follow through. There is no reason to chase anything in this market so I will be passive if this scenario plays out (20%). A gradual drift higher on the open with mixed overlapping candles would be a sign of weak trend strength. When that move stalls, a good shorting opportunity would set up. Look for a bearish hammer/bearish engulf off of the high of the day as a sign that a reversal is pending. This scenario has a 20% chance of playing out. A more likely scenario is a bid check. The market tries to �ll in some of the overnight gap up. Mixed overlapping candles will be a sign that the trend strength during the dip is weak. That will give us time to �nd stocks with relative strength and we can separate the fakes from the real deal. Once the market �nds support we can expect a rally and it will be time to buy these stocks. We do not want the retracement to be deep (more than half of the gap up preserved) or to last more than an hour. If that happens it would suggest decent selling pressure. This scenario has a good chance of playing out and it presents the best opportunities for us (30%). A strong gap reversal would have long red candles and brief pauses. Half of the overnight gains would easily be stripped away. This would suggest that sellers are fairly aggressive. The gap �ll would be fairly deep and the pullback will take a couple of hours to run its course. In this scenario you would focus on shorts. We want the bounces to last less than 30 minutes. This scenario has a 20% chance of playing out. The �nal scenario is a complete gap reversal. Stacked long red candles consecutively in the �rst 30 minutes with little to no overlap would be a sign of heavy selling. We have seen decent buying and the big down gap reversal two days ago tells us that buyers are aggressive enough to prevent that. This scenario only has a 10% chance of playing out. It is critically important to get the longer term context and then to drill down to the shorter time frames. Understand the possible scenarios and know the characteristics of each one. When they start to unfold, you will know what to expect and what action you plan to take. You should also know which scenario is most desirable and which one is most likely (they are not always the same). The chart below is how the day actually played out. The scenario we got was not the one we wanted. Gap and go patterns force us to chase early in the day and that is never wise. We do not have time to properly vet (observe) stocks and it is di�cult to separate the real from the fake. This pattern also has a tendency to run to its destination and compress. That makes it di�cult to trade the rest of the day. That means we have to trade smaller size early (because we don’t ever want to chase) so that we can make some money early in the day. It also means that we should take gains after 90 minutes of trading because the rest of the day the market will compress. Being able to read price action told us which scenario was going to play out and what actions we should take. The SPY stayed in that tight compression the rest of the day and there was a breakout in the last 10 minutes of trading. In the recording, you can clearly hear these predictions after 15 minutes of trading. I’m not clairvoyant, I just know how to read price action. **Rule 1 — Trend Identification**:

> "When price breaks below the lower boundary of a compression zone on heavy volume, there is a brief window to carry overnight shorts. This is the transition phase — the only optimal swing trade window in this type of downtrend."

## 1. WHAT IS SHOWN

This is a **15-minute (M15) candlestick chart of SPY (S&P 500 ETF)** spanning approximately one trading week from **June 17 through June 23**. The price range covers roughly $362 to $378.50. A volume indicator appears at the bottom (SPY:VOLUME = 5553100). The chart is from OneOption.com (watermark visible).

The overall price action shows:
- A dramatic sell-off/low around June 17 (near $362-363)
- A massive bounce/reversal
- A gap up on June 21
- A gap down testing the prior day's gains
- A powerful gap fill and rally on June 22 with stacked green candles
- Choppy, two-sided trading on June 23 near the highs (~$376-378)

This chart serves as the **M15 drill-down** referenced in the book page, where the author starts with the longer-term price action, zooms into M15, and then further into M5.

---

## 2. ANNOTATIONS INVENTORY (Exhaustive)

### Annotation 1: "Gap up" (with arrow)
- **Color/Style:** Blue text with a blue arrow pointing right toward the candles
- **Location:** Bottom-left area, pointing to the green candles on June 17 afternoon
- **What it marks:** The initial gap up move off the lows. The candles show a strong upward move from around $363 to approximately $368-369

### Annotation 2: "Gap and go is a sign that buyers are interested" (with arrow)
- **Color/Style:** Blue text with a blue arrow pointing right
- **Location:** Upper-left area, pointing to the continuation candles after the initial gap up on June 17
- **What it marks:** After the gap up, price continued higher rather than filling the gap — this "gap and go" pattern signals genuine buyer interest and momentum

### Annotation 3: "Big bounce off of a new 52-week low resulting in a D1 doji. That could signal a reversal"
- **Color/Style:** Blue text with a blue arrow pointing up to the lowest candles
- **Location:** Bottom-left corner
- **What it marks:** The absolute low point around $362-363 on June 17. On the daily chart, this day printed a doji candle (open ≈ close) after hitting a new 52-week low — a classic potential reversal signal

### Annotation 4: "Dips and a compression after the initial surge suggest that sellers are present"
- **Color/Style:** Blue text at the top of the chart, with blue arrows pointing down to the price action on June 21
- **Location:** Points to the area after the gap up on June 21, where price made small dips and overlapping candles
- **What it marks:** After the initial surge on June 21, the candles show pullbacks and tight overlapping bars. This compression/overlap indicates sellers are pushing back — the trend is not clean, and both sides are engaged

### Annotation 5: "Big gap down tests the gains from the prior day. Are buyers still interested?"
- **Color/Style:** Blue text with blue arrows
- **Location:** Center-left area, pointing to the gap down opening on June 22 (around the $373-374 level)
- **What it marks:** The market gapped down significantly, testing whether the prior day's rally had real conviction. This poses a critical question: will buyers defend, or was the prior move a fake?

### Annotation 6: "Stacked green candles with little to no overlap. Very strong trend. Gap filled on first attempt and it blew thru the prior day's high"
- **Color/Style:** Blue text with blue arrows pointing to consecutive green candles
- **Location:** Center of the chart, pointing to the powerful rally on June 22
- **What it marks:** A series of stacked green (bullish) candles with minimal overlap between them — this is the hallmark of a **very strong trend**. The gap from the open was filled on the first attempt, and price broke through the prior day's high. This answers the question from Annotation 5 definitively: YES, buyers are very interested

### Annotation 7: "Fairly deep retracements so sellers are still engaged. Expect choppy trading"
- **Color/Style:** Blue text with blue arrows
- **Location:** Center-right area, pointing to price action on June 22 afternoon / June 23 morning
- **What it marks:** After the strong rally, the pullbacks (retracements) became deeper — candles were pulling back more than half of the prior move. This indicates sellers are now actively fighting buyers, and the easy trending is over. The expectation shifts to **choppy, two-sided action**

### Annotation 8: "Headfake" (with horizontal bracket/arrow)
- **Color/Style:** Blue text with a blue horizontal bracket/line
- **Location:** Top of the chart, spanning a section around June 22 close / June 23 open where price briefly broke above a level then reversed
- **What it marks:** Price briefly pushed above the resistance zone (a false breakout or "headfake"), then pulled back. This is a trap for breakout buyers

### Annotation 9: "Resistance" (with horizontal line)
- **Color/Style:** Blue text with a blue horizontal line extending right
- **Location:** Top of chart, approximately at the $378-378.40 level
- **What it marks:** A clear resistance level that price struggled to break above. The horizontal line shows where sellers consistently capped advances. This becomes the key level for June 23 trading

### Annotation 10: "Going into Thursday I expected choppy trading. Buyers and sellers were battling it out. There was support at the closing price from Wed and resistance at the high from Wed. The market is in a longer term down trend, but we were due for a relief bounce after the gap and go Tues. Expect 2-sided action and look for reversals."
- **Color/Style:** Blue text block
- **Location:** Right side of the chart, describing the June 23 (Thursday) trading context
- **What it marks:** This is the author's **pre-market analysis and prediction** for Thursday. It establishes:
  - Support = Wednesday's closing price
  - Resistance = Wednesday's high
  - Context = longer-term downtrend, but short-term relief bounce
  - Strategy = expect two-sided/choppy action, trade reversals not breakouts

- **Blue arrows** on June 22 pointing to individual stacked green candles
- **Vertical dotted lines** separating trading days
- **Price scale** on the right

# Detailed Chart Analysis: SPY M5 (5-Minute) Chart — Gap and Go with Compression

---

## 1. WHAT IS SHOWN

This is a **5-minute candlestick chart of SPY (S&P 500 ETF)** labeled "SPY - M5" in the upper left corner. The chart covers what appears to be portions of two trading sessions (likely the prior day's close and the current day's open and first few hours of trading). A volume histogram and what appears to be a momentum indicator (possibly MACD or a similar oscillator) are plotted below the main price panel.

The overall price action shows:
- A prior trading session with mixed/choppy red and green candles in the **$374–$378 range**
- An **overnight gap up** opening significantly higher, around **$380+**
- A strong initial rally with **stacked green candles** moving from approximately $380 to $385+
- A transition into a **tight compression/consolidation zone** near the highs around **$386–$387**

The price ultimately reaches into the upper $386–$387 area where it enters a clearly marked compression phase.

---

## 2. ANNOTATIONS INVENTORY

### Annotation 1: "Compression" (top of chart)
- **Location:** Upper right portion of the chart, with a **shaded blue/purple rectangular zone** highlighting the tight range of candles near the session highs
- **What it marks:** A cluster of small-bodied, overlapping candles that are trading in a narrow horizontal range after a strong upward move. The candles within the box are small, mixed red and green, showing equilibrium between buyers and sellers
- **Style:** Text label with a shaded rectangular box overlay encompassing approximately 8–10 candles

### Annotation 2: Long text callout (left side of chart)
- **Exact text:** "Long green candle, very little retracement, long green candle. 3 bars in I knew we were going to get a gap and go. I also said that we have another hour of upside and then we are going to compress."
- **Location:** Left side of the chart with an **arrow pointing right** toward the early candles of the gap-up session — specifically pointing to the first 3 candles after the gap up opened
- **What it marks:** The initial price action after the gap up — identifying the critical **first three bars** of the session. These bars show: (1) a long green candle, (2) a very small retracement candle, (3) another long green candle. This three-bar sequence was the signal that confirmed the gap-and-go pattern
- **Style:** White/light text on dark background, with a horizontal arrow pointing to the specific candles

### Annotation 3: "Gap up →"
- **Location:** Center-right area of the chart, with an arrow pointing to the **gap between the prior session's close and the current session's open**
- **What it marks:** The literal price gap — the space between where the prior day's trading ended (around $376–$378) and where the new day opened (around $380). This is a clearly visible vertical space with no candles
- **Style:** Simple text with a right-pointing arrow

### Annotation 4: Shaded/boxed zone around the first few candles
- **Location:** There appears to be a **rectangular highlight/box** around the first 2-3 candles after the gap up
- **What it marks:** The critical "read zone" — the first three bars that confirmed the gap-and-go pattern

### Annotation 5: Volume bars (bottom panel)
- Mixed green and red volume bars, with notably **higher volume on the green candles** during the initial gap-up rally, and **declining/lighter volume** during the compression phase

### Annotation 6: Oscillator/Indicator (bottom sub-panel)
- A line-based indicator (possibly MACD) showing momentum that appears to peak during the strong move up and then flatten during compression

---

## 3. PATTERN OR CONCEPT BEING TAUGHT

### Pattern: **Gap and Go → Compression**

This chart illustrates the **Gap and Go** pattern and, critically, what happens **after** the initial move — the transition into **compression**.

From the surrounding book context, the author describes several scenarios for how SPY might behave at the $380 resistance level. The scenario that actually played out was a **gap-and-go** — but importantly, the author emphasizes this was **not the preferred scenario** because gap-and-go patterns are:
- Difficult to distinguish from fakes early in the day
- They force traders to chase, which is "never wise"
- The pattern tends to run to its destination and then compress
- It makes the rest of the day difficult to trade

### The Rules:

**Rule 1 — Confirmation in 3 Bars:**
> "When the market gaps up and the first three bars show: long green candle → very little retracement → long green candle, THEN a gap-and-go is confirmed."

**Rule 2 — Time-Based Expectation:**
> "When a gap-and-go is confirmed, expect approximately one hour of upside movement, THEN expect the market to compress (trade in a tight range for the rest of the day)."

**Rule 3 — Trade Sizing for Gap-and-Go:**
> "When you identify a gap-and-go, trade smaller size early because you cannot easily separate the real move from the fake. Do not chase."

**Rule 4 — Post-Move Compression:**
> "When the initial gap-and-go move exhausts itself, expect tight compression. This compression makes it difficult to trade the rest of the day — accept this and reduce activity."

**Rule 5 — Time Constraint:**
> "When trading a gap-and-go, take gains after 90 minutes of trading because the rest of the day the market will compress."

### What a trader should DO:
- Read the first 3 candles carefully to identify the pattern
- Trade smaller size because gap-and-go is hard to confirm vs. fakes
- Take profits within the first 60–90 minutes
- Once compression begins, **stop trading** or significantly reduce expectations
- Watch for a potential breakout in the last 10 minutes of the day (as mentioned in the book text)

### What a trader should AVOID:
- **Do NOT chase** the gap-and-go early in the day
- Do NOT continue trading aggressively once compression sets in
- Do NOT confuse a gap-and-go with other scenarios (the author outlines 4-5 possible scenarios and emphasizes knowing which one is playing out)

---

## 4. MY UNDERSTANDING — Core Insights

### The Deep Insight: **Pattern Recognition Within the First 15 Minutes Dictates the Entire Day**

The author explicitly states: *"You can clearly hear these predictions after 15 minutes of trading."* This is the crux

Customize appearance Volume Reveals Conviction | OneOption - Stocks & Options Trading Suite Volume Reveals Conviction Market First 10 min read 2025-01-28 Heavy volume moves tell us that the move is legitimate and light volume tells us it can’t be trusted. Almost every technical indicator has two components: price and volume. That alone should tell you how important volume is to our technical analysis. Volume is very easy to analyze and it is either heavy, average or light. It does not require lengthy explanations so it does not get the attention it deserves. Consequently, it is overlooked by novice traders. Let’s not make the mistake of glossing over this topic. VOLUME CONVEYS VERY IMPORTANT INFORMATION AND IT NEEDS TO BE A MAJOR PART OF YOUR TECHNICAL ANALYSIS! I hope that got your attention. Volume tells us how excited buyers and sellers are. That in turn helps us gauge the strength of a trend. Our goal as traders is to predict price movement and sustained heavy volume helps us to determine direction. If a manufacturer reduced the price of their product there would be no way to measure the success/failure of the promotion without volume. They wouldn’t know if the product is moving or sitting on the shelves. Volume helps them determine the demand for it at that price and how much of it they need to produce. If the product is �ying off of the shelves and the line is out the door and around the corner, they can safely predict that this promotion will be successful. We can’t assess the quality of a market move without looking at volume. What if there is light volume and no move? This is common when the market is compressing in a tight range. It is a sign of equilibrium and neither side has an advantage. At some point a news item will spark a breakout one way or the other. Set alerts above and below the compression and wait. Since there is light volume, the trading range could last a long time. What if there is heavy volume and no move? This is a good scenario. The heavy volume indicates that buyers and sellers are interested. Shortly, one side or the other will prevail and that breakout is likely to have follow through (“legs”). On the breakout, the losing side will scramble to adjust and the winning side will add to positions. The breakout on volume will hit everyone’s radar and the frenzy is on! Custom Search in Option Stalker Pro will �nd stocks with heavy volume that are in a compression. Set your alerts above and below the compression and wait for the breakout. Why do light volume rallies happen? We often see light volume rallies at the end of a long term uptrend. Because the trend is strong, sellers are extremely passive and they are holding out for a higher price. Even a small buyer can drive the price higher. Imagine this attitude on the part of the seller, “If you want it, come and get it at this nice high price. If you are not interested at that level, I will just hang on to it.” This is what we call a sellers boycott. They are simply not interested in selling unless they get what they consider to be a premium. At that high price, buyers are not willing to load up so the volume remains light. A light volume spike to a new high could be a buying climax so pay attention to those because a drop is likely very soon. Of course, a light volume trend lower in a bear market would indicate that buyers are not interested. They are expecting lower prices and they will wait for signs of support. This is a “buyer boycott” and it can be characterized by this attitude, “If you are that anxious to sell, come and get me all the way down here.” Why do light volume bounces happen? When we refer to a “bounce”, it suggests that the rebound is temporary and that the longer term down trend will prevail. Most traders don’t understand bounces. “Why is anyone buying this crap when the market is clearly going down?” The market does not go straight up or straight down. At some point during a big decline, short sellers will start taking pro�ts. That buying provides support and other short sellers will also start to take gains. This will cause a bounce. Institutions are always “testing the water” and they can spark short term bounces as well. They will try to spark short covering to shake traders out of positions. Remember, short sellers are looking for signs of support because they are eager to take gains. The institutions are more interested in the magnitude and the duration of the bounce. They are constantly trying to gauge how aggressive buyers and sellers are and they watch volume very closely. A brief and shallow light volume bounce that only lasts six bars will tell them that the selling pressure is heavy. The institutions will exit what they bought and short even more. They don’t care if they lost money trying to spark a bounce because that will provide them with important information. Chances are, if the longer term trend is down, they have huge short positions. If the bounce has good height and big volume, there is a likelihood that it could last a long time. In that event, they will start reducing longer term short positions. The same principles I’ve described would apply to light volume dips in the context of a longer term up trend. Does a light volume rally mean sell short? Absolutely not! Light volume in and of itself does not constitute a trading opportunity. These moves can continue for long periods of time and they can in�ict incredible pain if you are early. Sometimes, the volume will increase during the move and it will transition into a legitimate trend. How should we swing trade heavy volume declines? If the market is in a long term down trend it will be con�rmed by heavy volume. Your objective is to short bounces when they stall and break technical support. Take gains during big drops and go to cash. Repeat. During bounces you can evaluate the magnitude of the bounce and the volume. If the height of the bounce recaptures much of the recent decline (rally above the open from a previous long red candle) and if it comes on heavy volume, it is likely to last a while. If the move starts to gain traction, you can join it with small size (relative to your recent short positions) and know that this is going to be a short term trade. Be ready to take gains at the �rst sign of trouble and be ready to go short on a technical breakdown. For most swing traders who can’t watch the market during the day, I would discourage this tactic. You are “getting cute” and trading against the longer term down trend. When the bounce reverses you will be scrambling to exit longs instead of focusing on entering short positions. If the bounce is shallow and the volume is light, it is not likely to last long. That would be a sign that sellers are still nearby and you might need to re-establish your short position quickly. Watch for these tiny bounces when the momentum is very strong (stacked red candles) and try to stick with the short position. That price action tells us that sellers are very aggressive. Use these same concepts (in reverse) during heavy volume long term up trends. In a strong up trend, swing traders want to “buy dips and sell rips”. How long can light volume moves last? The Fed printed money like mad after the 2008-2009 �nancial crisis and credit risk was low for a decade. Bond yields were near 0% and investors had to stay in equities to generate a return. Corporations were issuing cheap debt and using the proceeds to buy back shares. These forces kept a very strong bid to the market and the dips were brief and shallow. The end result was a very light volume rally that lasted for nearly a decade. Don’t discount the longevity of light volume moves. Draw your trendlines and wait for those technical breaches. So let’s take a look at the volume during the last year and how it helped us to determine which side to be on. The context of the chart below is that the market was in a VERY strong two-year up trend and that it was starting to transition to a bear market. To this point, the dips were brief and shallow. Notice how the drops came on heavy volume and the rallies came on light volume. Initially, the bounces had nice height. Long term bull markets die hard because buyers are still trained to buy dips. 1OVol is our proprietary indicator. If it is above zero, the volume is greater than the 20-period average. If it is below zero, it is below average. When the market bounced in the chart below, the heavy volume only lasted a day or two. When the market dropped, the volume was heavy for many days in a row. The rally at the beginning of the chart took place on light volume. There were only a few days where it spiked. The bounce lasted for a month and it had good height. Traders that tried to stick with short positions took extreme “heat”. Some did not expect the bounce to last so long or to bounce so high so they exited short positions. That probably extended the life of the bounce. When that up trendline was breached, the selling pressure was fast and furious and the S&P 500 lost almost 1000 points (large shaded blue area). In the last two months the market has staged another light volume rally. Notice how there are only a few heavy volume days within this move. Seasonal strength could fuel the move into year-end. Don’t be early with short positions, but know that a nasty drop is looming. During light volume contra trend moves you want to be in cash or in very small positions. Heavy volume is a sign of conviction and it helps us to predict direction. That said, I do use it for con�rmation on a longer term basis so I want to introduce it. Like most indicators it has a fast line (1OP2, default color: red) and a slow line (1OP1, default color: blue). When the fast line crosses the slow line, a trade signal is generated. Under ideal conditions the indicator will have cycles with nice tall peaks and deep troughs. When the indicator is in a deep trough and 1OP2 crosses above 1OP1, a buy signal is generated. - **Lower panel**: The proprietary **1OP indicator** consisting of two lines — a solid line (fast line, called "10P2" in the text, default red) and a dotted/dashed line (slow line, called "10P", default blue)

### Annotation 1 — First Circle (Far Left, Bottom of Indicator Panel)
- **Location**: A **blue circle** drawn around the area where the solid line (fast) crosses below the dotted line (slow) at the far left of the indicator panel, during a deep trough well below zero.

### Annotation 2 — Second Circle (Center-Left, Bottom of Indicator Panel)
- **Location**: A **blue circle** drawn around the crossover point where the solid line crosses above the dotted line after a deep trough, roughly in the center-left of the indicator panel. The indicator is well below zero at this point (approximately -15 to -20 range).
- **Associated Text Label**: *"After a deep trough the solid line crosses above the dotted line producing a buy signal"*
- **What it marks**: The **buy signal** generated when the fast line crosses above the slow line after the indicator has made a deep trough. This coincides with the transition from the **pink/red zone to the green zone** on the chart.
- **Price action correspondence**: The price bottoms around $370.50 and begins a sustained upward move.

### Annotation 3 — Third Annotation with Arrow (Center-Right of Indicator Panel)
- **Location**: A **blue arrow** pointing downward to a specific area in the indicator panel where both lines are hovering near or slightly below the zero line, during the ongoing green (bullish) zone on the right side of the chart.
- **Associated Text Label**: *"We want the indicator to get above zero before considering this a bearish cycle. This would still be considered part of a long bullish cycle"*
- **What it marks**: A moment where the indicator lines dip slightly or flatten near the zero line without the fast line having first risen meaningfully above zero. Despite what might look like a mini crossover or weakening, the annotation explicitly states this should **NOT** be treated as a new bearish cycle. It remains part of the **existing long bullish cycle**.
- **Price action correspondence**: Price consolidates and has some mixed candles (red and green) in the $374-$376 range before continuing higher, confirming that this was indeed still a bullish environment.

### Background Shading
- **Pink/Red zones**: Two pink/red shaded areas on the left portion of the chart, indicating **bearish cycles** where the 1OP is signaling downside.
- **Green zones**: A large green shaded area dominating the right two-thirds of the chart, indicating a **bullish cycle** where the 1OP is signaling upside.
- The transition points between colors correspond to the crossover signals circled in the annotations.

### Zero Line
- A **horizontal dashed line** at the 0.00 level in the indicator panel, serving as the critical reference level discussed in Annotation 3.

### Volume Bars
- At the very bottom of the chart, there are small **volume bars** (teal/green colored), showing trading volume per period.

---

## 3. PATTERN OR CONCEPT BEING TAUGHT

This chart teaches **three critical concepts** about the 1OP indicator:

### Concept A: Sell Signal Generation
**Rule**: *"When the 1OP fast line (solid) crosses BELOW the slow line (dotted) after a spike upward, a SELL signal is generated."*

The trader should watch for the indicator to spike up (forming a peak), and then when the fast line rolls over and crosses below the slow line, this marks the beginning of a bearish cycle (pink zone). This is when a trader should consider short positions or exiting longs.

### Concept B: Buy Signal Generation
**Rule**: *"When the 1OP fast line (solid) crosses ABOVE the slow line (dotted) after a deep trough, a BUY signal is generated."*

The trader should watch for the indicator to plunge down (forming a deep trough), and then when the fast line turns up and crosses above the slow line, this marks the beginning of a bullish cycle (green zone). This is when a trader should consider long positions or exiting shorts.

### Concept C: The Zero Line Rule for Cycle Validation (MOST IMPORTANT)
**Rule**: *"When the indicator has not risen above zero during a bullish cycle and the lines begin to flatten or slightly cross near zero, do NOT consider this a new bearish cycle. The indicator must get above zero first before a subsequent bearish crossover can be considered a valid new bearish cycle."*

This is the nuanced rule being emphasized. Not every crossover is a valid signal. The indicator must complete a **full cycle** — meaning it needs to move meaningfully above zero during a bullish cycle before a bearish crossover carries weight. If it stays below or near zero, the bullish cycle is still considered intact.

---

## 4. MY UNDERSTANDING — CORE INSIGHTS

### The Deep Insight: Cycle Completion and the Zero Line as a Filter

The most important teaching on this chart is **Annotation 3** — the zero line filter. This is what separates a novice 1OP user from a skilled one. Here's why:

**The problem it solves**: In any dual-line crossover indicator system (similar in concept to MACD), there are frequent mini-crossovers, especially when momentum is weak or price is consolidating. A naive trader who acts on every crossover will get **whipsawed** — constantly entering and exiting positions during noise, accumulating losses.

**The solution**: The 1OP uses the zero line as a **cycle validation threshold**. A bullish cycle isn't "complete" until the indicator has risen above zero. Only after the indicator has been above zero can a subsequent bearish crossover be treated as a legitimate new bearish cycle. This prevents the trader from prematurely flipping to a bearish bias during what is actually a consolidation within an ongoing bullish move.

### Why This Setup is Valid
In this specific chart, the buy signal (Annotation 2) came from a **deep trough** — well below zero around -15 to -20. Deep troughs represent strong bearish momentum that has exhausted itself, making the subsequent bullish crossover a high-conviction signal. The text on the book page confirms: *"We like nice deep troughs, big spikes and defined crosses."*

The price then rallied significantly from ~$370.50 to ~$376.50, which is a substantial intraday move. During this rally, the indicator stayed near or below zero — it never made a meaningful spike above zero. This tells us the bullish momentum, while present in price, hasn't yet fully expressed itself in the indicator's cycle. Therefore, any downward crossover near zero is **premature** and should not be acted upon.

### What Would Make This Invalid (i.e., a True Bearish Signal)
If the indicator had:
1. Risen well **above zero** (creating a visible spike/peak above the zero line)
2. Then the fast line crossed below the slow line from that elevated position

...THEN it would be a valid bearish signal and the green zone would end. The key distinction is: **the cycle must complete (cross above zero) before the opposite signal can be trusted.**

### Connecting to the Broader Book Context
From the surrounding page text, this connects to the concept of **"benign" cycles** — when a cycle doesn't produce meaningful price movement, the next cycle in the opposite direction is more likely to produce. The text also emphasizes that when 1OP has many **mini crosses** near the zero line, the market trend strength is poor, price action is choppy, and the trader should **reduce trading activity**. The zero line proximity and lack of defined cycles is a warning to stay patient.

### Practical Trader Takeaway
- **Trade the deep troughs and big spikes** — these are high-conviction signals
- **Ignore crossovers near the zero line** that haven't completed a full cycle
- **The zero line is your filter** — it separates real cycle transitions from noise
- **When in doubt, stay with the current cycle** until the indicator proves otherwise by completing a full oscillation above/below zero
- This indicator is designed for **short-term/day trading** and should be combined with technical confirmation on longer-term analysis

If a bullish cycle doesn't produce, it means buyers couldn't gain control — the path of least resistance remains down. This is analogous to how in physics, potential energy converts to kinetic energy. A benign cycle is stored potential energy.

- If the "benign" bullish cycle actually produced a modest rally but you dismissed it — you might be misreading the cycle

This chart teaches traders to think in **probabilities and sequences** rather than isolated signals. ### Concept B: Mini Crosses Signal Weak/Unreliable Conditions

**Rule: "When 1OP has lots of small, tight crosses near the zero line (mini crosses), the trend strength is weak, the indicator is unreliable, and a trader should reduce position size or avoid trading the indicator signals."**

- The ideal 1OP pattern has **nice high spikes, deep troughs, and clean crosses** — this gives clean, tradeable signals.
- Mini crosses indicate: choppy/range-bound price action, tight ranges, low volume, mixed candles — a **compression** environment.
- A trader should: **Keep trading to a minimum** during mini-cross periods, not rely on the indicator, and recognize that a compression/breakout may be forthcoming.

### Concept C: Benign Cycles (from page context)

The page text also introduces the concept of **"benign" cycles** — when the market is flat during a bullish cycle, that cycle did not produce. A cycle that does not produce is called benign, and it increases the probability that the **next bearish cross will be a good one**. Each passing benign cycle that doesn't produce increases the odds that the next one will.

---

### The Deep Insight: 1OP Is a Trend-Confirmation Tool, Not a Reversal Signal

# Analysis of the 1OP Indicator Chart — SPY Daily

## 1. WHAT IS SHOWN

This is a **daily candlestick chart of SPY (S&P 500 ETF)** showing price action from approximately **mid-June through mid-November**. The price ranges from roughly 350 to 425. The chart displays:
