## 2. ANNOTATIONS INVENTORY — Exhaustive List

### Annotation 1: Bullish Divergence Callout (Upper Left)
- **Exact text:** *"This is a bullish divergence. The market is moving higher during a bearish cycle. This is a sign that the trend is strong and the next bullish cycle should produce"*
- **Color/style:** Blue text with a blue arrow pointing from the text box to the price action during a **red/pink shaded zone** (bearish cycle) in the late June to mid-July period
- **What it marks:** During the red-shaded bearish 1OP cycle (approximately late June through mid-July), the price was actually moving **higher** — the market rallied from approximately 375 to 390 even though the 1OP indicator was in a bearish cycle. The arrow specifically points to the upward price movement within the red zone. This divergence between the indicator signal (bearish) and actual price movement (bullish) is highlighted as a sign of underlying bullish trend strength.

### Annotation 2: Weak Trend Strength Callout (Lower Right)
- **Exact text:** *"Lots of little crosses are a sign of weak trend strength and the indicator is not reliable. We want nice high spikes, deep troughs and clean crosses"*
- **Color/style:** Blue text positioned in the lower portion of the 1OP indicator panel, with **multiple small blue arrows** pointing down to specific locations on the 1OP oscillator lines
- **What it marks:** From approximately late August through November, the 1OP indicator shows numerous **small, choppy crosses** between the fast and slow lines. The arrows (approximately 6-7 of them) point to individual instances where the 1OP lines cross but with very shallow amplitude — the oscillator stays relatively flat and close to the zero/center line rather than making pronounced peaks and troughs. This contrasts sharply with the left portion of the chart (June-August) where the 1OP had wide, clean swings.

- **Color/style:** Light red/pink background shading spanning the full chart height
- **What they mark:** Periods when the 1OP indicator is in a **bearish cycle**. Major red zones appear:
  - Late June through mid-July (the period where the bullish divergence is noted)

- **What it marks:** The instrument (SPY), current price (396.10), and timeframe (D1 = Daily)

**Rule: "When the market moves higher during a bearish 1OP cycle, this is a bullish divergence — it confirms the uptrend is strong and the next bullish cycle should produce significant gains."**

Make sure that when the prior day high is breached, the candles are stacked and green. The volume needs to be heavy and you want to take out that high early in the day. When we break through the prior day low, we want to do it early in the day and on heavy volume. We need those stacked red candles. If the candles are mixed and they are scattered the prior day’s range, the market is not ready and there is no clear direction. In the charts below I featured two long candles. The red one is closing on its low of the day and there is no tail (a small tail is �ne). This is a sign of heavy selling right into the close. We want those long candles preserved. After a big move down, the SPY will usually take a break the next day and it will be an “inside day”. It is fairly uncommon to see big days back-to-back and you will notice this if you look at a D1 chart. Ideally, the mid-point from the long red candle is preserved. The candle the next day can be green or red. They are usually pretty small. Often there will be a small bounce and that is why I colored it green. Two or three days after that long red candle you should watch for follow through selling and that is the M5 pattern you want. Stacked red candles on volume through the low from that red candle will signal that sellers are back. The SPY was not able to rally above the mid-point so sellers were never far away. In the chart on the right we have a giant green candle that closed on the high of the day (no wick). There can be a small wick, we just want to see that relentless buying right into the close. The next day will be an “inside day” and we want half of the long green candle preserved. There will often be a little pro�t taking and that is why I colored it red. Two or three days after that long green candle we will see follow through buying and we want to see those stacked green candles on volume blow through the high from the long green candle. That is a sign that buyers are back. One �nal note. If the intraday move is very steep (60 degrees or more), it is not sustainable. When you see long candles that are erased (at the high or low), take gains. Sharp moves like this will often produce a large contra move. The strength of the �rst move is legitimate, the contra move is not. Wait for the contra move to stall and you will get “another bite from the apple”. If the initial intraday move has a very gradual slope, you will have opportunities to build a position, add to it and ride it. On the left side of the chart below you will see a sharp initial drop. This is going to produce a tall bounce and you need to take gains when the long red candle at the low of the day is erased by two green candles. When that move stalled, there was an opportunity to short on the rejection from VWAP (it is anchored to the �rst trade of the day). On the right side of the screen shot below you can see that a nice gradual drift lower is forming and how the SPY was not able to get above VWAP . When that resistance held, we were able to add to the trade and we also had an opportunity to add at the prior day’s low. The recent trend and the prior day’s candle provide us with important information about what we should expect today. We conduct pre-open research and we determine where the market is likely to open based on the overnight session. If the open is projected to be outside of the previous day’s range, we identify other key price levels that might be in play. If it is fairly tight to the prior days range (or inside of it) we use the open, high, low, close and midpoint to guide us. We know the bullish and bearish M5 patterns to watch for and we formulate a game plan. As this nice, tight orderly patterns are forming, we scale in. We don’t trade mixed overlapping candles on light volume particularly if the market is going to open inside of the prior day’s range. The price action today is going to provide us with valuable information when we set up our game plan tomorrow. The context in this lesson was very short- term in nature. This is where it gets exciting. We are going to zoom out in the next lesson and you are going to be able to visualize what the intraday M5 price action probably looked just by looking at a longer-term D1 chart.

Customize appearance Framing Today's Session | OneOption - Stocks & Options Trading Suite If we know what to expect, we can be proactive. Our short-term analysis for the S&P 500 has focused on price action to this point. Your ability to gauge buying and selling pressure is by far your top priority and it will have the greatest impact on your success. Tight, orderly trends where candles of a single color have little overlap are ideal if they come on heavy volume. We expect those trends to cut through key price levels with ease. When that happens we have technical con�rmation and we can enter and add to our trades. In an up trend, red candles are quickly erased by green candles and that gives us additional con�rmation along the way. There is no substitute for this analysis across multiple time frames. We can’t stop there. The information in this article will help us visualize the most likely price action for the day ahead. Moves unfold very quickly and our goal is to be proactive. “Inside Days” When the market can’t get below the prior day’s low or above the prior day’s high, we call that an “inside day”. These two minor levels represent the very �rst support and resistance. If they remain intact, the price action will be choppy and the volume will be light. This means that buy and sell programs will dominate the action and our odds of success decrease. Just as a move gains traction, the rug will get pulled out. Breaching the prior day’s range is the minimum requirement for a good trading conditions, but we still need above average volume and nice orderly candles. If the market can’t penetrate these minor price levels in the �rst two hours, you should err on the side of not trading /ES. This generalization applies when the previous day’s range was normal and when the opening price today was inside of that range. Declining ATR – A technical study called ATR (average true range) measures the intraday ranges and I like using a 20-day moving average. If the ranges have been collapsing, the value will decline. This warns you that big moves are less likely. A breakout through the prior day’s range doesn’t guarantee that the price action will be good. That is an easy hurdle to clear because the market doesn’t have to move very far. We need to see stacked candles of a single color on volume if the market does clear the prior day’s range. If we don’t have that, the breakout is less likely to hold. Rising ATR – If the 20-day ATR has been expanding, the intraday ranges have been wide and volatility is increasing. Typically, the volume will be heavy and the D1 candles will be long. This is the exception where you can still have good intraday price action during an “inside day”. Nice sweeping moves within the prior day’s range with candles of a single color are what we want to see on good volume. Both sides are likely to be active. Long Bodies These candles are easy to spot and they will stand out on a D1 chart. A move that’s 1.5 times the 20-day average true range (or more) that closes near the high/low would qualify. If the candle is green, we want a relatively small wick. If the candle is red, we want a relatively small tail. Why is this important? We one side to completely dominate the entire session with little to no retracement into the closing bell. That show of power is going to help us predict future price movement. These moves often gain momentum during the day and they are exaggerated. Speculators are �ushed out of positions, stops are triggered and buy/sell programs kick in. Traders digest the move the next day and they will determine how much of it was “legitimate”. Buyers and sellers will pair off the next day and “programs” will probe for support/resistance in search of “size”. If the market tanked the previous day, we often see a small gap up the next morning (bearish speculators take pro�ts). Longer-term sellers are not going to “throw in the towel” and any move higher will be stubborn. That increases the odds that the bounce will not be very “tall” and most of the prior day’s losses will be preserved (chart below). If the market surged higher the prior day, we will often see small gaps down overnight (pro�t taking). We should expect good support and any move lower is likely to be choppy with mixed overlapping candles. Buyers were in control yesterday and they are lurking. Here are some important notes about “Big Candles”. 1. They are easy to spot and they serve as landmarks on the the daily chart. The open, high, low, close, and midpoint become short-term support and resistance levels. The ease (or struggle) to get through these points will help us gauge the strength of buyers and sellers. 2. It’s rare to see back-to-back long candles of the same color. Don’t take my word for it, look at a D1 chart. How many do you see? This is important information because it helps us set our expectations for the next day. 3. The day after the long body we want to preserve virtually all of the move. That would demonstrate that the move was legitimate and that we are likely to see follow through in that direction (charts below). 4. The day after the long body, steady retracement into that body and a close near the midpoint would be a sign that it was “fabricated”. Stops were triggered, speculators were �ushed out and programs kicked in. Now the contra side is expressing interest. 5. The long body was an incredible trend day and we traded it aggressively because we had stacked candles of a single color on heavy volume. We won’t know if the move was legitimate for another day. Here’s an exercise. Look for long bodies on a D1 chart. Was there signi�cant retracement the next day? What was the price action after that? Look for both situations. Your conclusions will help you frame the trading session that comes two days after the long bodied candle. �. Long green bodied candles are more likely to appear near relative lows. Back-to-back long bodied greens are rare and we should only look for them after a market down trend. They signal that a D1 trend reversal is likely. Remember the capitulation lows ? Long red bodied candles are more likely to appear near relative highs. Back-to-back long bodied reds are very rare and we will see them near all-time highs. Something major has happened and the news will dominate the headlines. It’s hard to rattle buyers to this degree when the 100- year trend has been so strong (that’s why they are rare). Don’t take my word for it, look for these patterns on a D1 chart. Long bodied candles are important. One side has dominated the other and they are going to help us plan our trading in the days to come. The very next day we should expect a day of rest. Buy and sell programs will dominate the action and they will probe for support and resistance. That means the “day after” is likely to be of low quality. If a lot of the body was retraced the next day, it is a sign that the move was largely fabricated. If much of the body was preserved the next day, we can expect follow through. These long bodied D1 candles will help us frame the next two trading days. Major Moving Averages & Longer-term Trendlines When major moving averages and longer-term trendlines can be reached during the day, they will act as magnets. That’s great news because this information helps us extend our targets. Without that moving average, we might have set lower targets. Now that it’s “in play”, we can take gains when it gets there. When we are planning our trading day and a major moving average is within two ATRs (20-day average true range) we know that it’s within striking distance and we know the odds of moving in that direction are higher. In general, we should treat major moving averages as if they are going to hold. During a normal D1 pullback in a bullish market, a choppy move lower with mixed overlapping candles indicates that buyers are engaged. We should expect that the moving average is going to hold. A jump off of that moving average (or slightly above it) will be a clear sign that buyers are interested. This information will help us frame our day trades for a week or more. That “pop” tells us that we can expect follow through. Buyers see this as a great opportunity. If the market tests the moving average and it sits above it for a few days, it is going to hold, buy buyers are not quite as aggressive. That information also helps us frame future trading days. We can expect a bounce, but not with the same vigor so we would trade smaller size. A small poke through a moving average and a close below it is simply a test. We don’t know how this is going to be resolved so we have to wait. This is a time to use extreme caution. Traders often assume that this is bearish and they start shorting. If the move is fake the market will �y back above the moving average. Bearish speculators were lured in and the trap worked. When they cover their shorts it will fuel the bounce. Breakouts and breakdowns get our attention, but that’s not where we make money. We make money on the follow through and we must wait for con�rmation. The longer the market spends below the moving average, the more likely it is to serve as resistance. It is a sign that sellers are still reducing risk and that the next support level will be tested. If the market gaps through a major moving average on heavy volume right on the open, it’s likely to be legitimate. You will see the overnight move before the market opens so you can plan for it. I’m not talking about a gap to the moving average, I’m talking about an overnight gap that is at least 20 /ES points through it. We want “escape velocity” from that price level right away. In all likelihood there was overnight news that is fueling this move. One side is excited and this is VERY likely to be a “Gap and Go” that results in a trend day. We don’t like to chase “Gap and Go’s”, but this is the exception. Start with a small position and add quickly on con�rmation. Ride the position the entire day and if the market closes on the the extreme (high of the day/low of the day), carry some of the position overnight. There will typically be follow through for a few days. This is all part of your pre-open analysis and we are using these odds to help us visualize the trading day that’s ahead of us. What is the most likely scenario that we will see today? Major Earnings Releases AAPL, AMZN, GOOG, MSFT, META, NVDA and TSLA are the largest market capitalization companies in the world and they account for more than 30% of the value for the S&P 500 as of this writing. These announcements will impact the market and most of them announce during the same week. If we are days out from these announcements, we know that the market bid should remain �rm since these stocks have been leading the market higher. Short sellers will be passive because the risk of a big rally is high. That means a big market drop is less likely. Traders will not place big bets either way ahead of the news and the intraday price action will be fairly dull with compressed daily ranges. This is important information because it helps us frame the trading day ahead. Once the earnings have been released, we gauge the reactions and we incorporated that information into our game plan. Are any of the stocks gapping through major price points? If they are, that move is likely to continue and that will impact the overall market. If the reactions are mixed, they will net each other out and the market impact could be negligible. Pending News Releases Pending news releases often result in dull trading the day before the announcement if they are signi�cant. We covered these in the Long- term Fundamental Section of the course. Traders will wait for the release and they will reduce their exposure into the news. The Unemployment Report and the FOMC statement are two examples. This information tells us to keep our trading light and to set passive day trading targets. On a swing basis, it means that we need to reduce risk because the reaction could produce a big market move. We trade the odds and we never guess the outcome of a binary event (50% odds). Why would we gamble on an outcome like this when we can predict price movement under normal conditions with odds greater than 75%? A good trader wouldn’t. There are some options strategies that you could use, but those trades are based on our opinion of the magnitude of the move, not the direction and I will discuss them in the Options Last section of the course. The FOMC statement is a “different animal”. As you know from the long-term fundamental section of the course, the market is driven by earnings and interest rates. When the Fed is maintaining a neutral posture (not raising or cutting), this event is benign. When the Fed is active (tightening or easing), the reactions are huge. This release comes out during the trading session so there’s no time to prepare. The �rst M5 candle could be an entire 20-day ATR. Minutes later, it could reverse. It’s often best to avoid this volatility. If you dare to trade it, go small. If there are two long stacked consecutive M5 candles with no retracement that both close on the extreme (high or low), there is a good chance that move will continue in that direction. It’s rare to see the pattern we have in the chart below. Typically there will be long bodied candles with overlap that have long tails and wicks. You should avoid trading this pattern because it re�ects uncertainty and the moves are huge. Often the Fed Chairman will hold a press conference 30 minutes after the statement is released. I have seen big initial moves reverse instantly once the press conference starts. If there is directional movement into the closing bell (higher or lower), don’t assume that it will continue the next day. There have been many times when it reverses overnight. Traders are able to digest the news and they feel differently once they’ve had a chance to re�ect. There are times when the FOMC statement happens just before Triple Witching and that increases the odds of a big move. Big pending news includes presidential elections and they happen every four years. You should expect lackluster trading a week or two before the election. Is there a bias after the election? In the age of arti�cial intelligence (AI), perhaps you should �nd out. It turns out that the inauguration also has a pattern. I’m not going to give you the answer. You’re a trader, go �nd out! Triple Witching Triple witching happens on the third Friday in March, June, September and December. This is when futures contracts, options on futures contracts and index options all expire. It is also a time when Asset Managers start “window dressing” for the end of the quarter. Indices are also rebalanced in June and December. Needless to say, institutions are busy adjusting their positions during these periods. It’s common to see at least one trend day during the week and we should expect more volatility and good volume. If the momentum during one of these sessions is established early in the day, you will see the nice tight orderly price action we look for. Trading programs take advantage of that intraday strength and they feed off of each other. This process fuels a strong directional move. If you understand that this could happen, you watch for it. First Day of the Month Statistically, the �rst day of the month has a bullish bias because retirement accounts and investment plans are structured to purchase assets on the �rst day of the month. Additionally, Social Security checks are issued and some of that money �ows into the market. This tendency is not a primary consideration, but it is another piece of information. This in�uence isn’t strong enough to offset selling during a bear market, but it does make a big drop less likely during a bullish market. Trading is all about the odds and this “tidbit” of information does have some utility. Seasonal Patterns Seasonal patterns are powerful. I have a trading axiom that I never swing short in November and December. Those are historically two of the strongest months of the year. To learn more about this, please read the article “Tis the Season” . September is historically one of the weakest months of the year. The Fed and politicians are in recess and the market gets nervous when no one is “minding shop”. August is typically one of the slowest months of the year. Traders take time off before their kids go back to school. These seasonal tendencies provide us with context and they will impact your short-term trading. Major Holidays Expect dull trading conditions the day before and the day after a holiday. Often, the two days before and the two days after the holiday are lackluster. If a holiday falls in the middle of the week, it can take a few trading days with it. The volume will completely dry up and the trading programs will dominate the action. Old news stories are recycled in an attempt to pump some excitement into the market and takeover rumors will swirl. This is all “fake” price action and the intent is to stir things up. When you see a holiday approaching, you should trade smaller size and you should expect compressed intraday trading ranges. Your odds of making money are low. Avoid unnecessary mistakes and take some time off. Heavy Volume I can’t conclude this article until I mention volume. When it’s above the 20-day average we know that institutions are participating and it legitimizes the move. Heavy volume declines with light volume bounces would indicate selling pressure. Heavy volume rallies with light volume drops would indicate buying pressure. If the volume is below average, the chances of a strong directional trend are less likely. Under these conditions we should expect sideways price action. If the market happens to trend on light volume, we should understand that these moves can easily be reversed. We need to be aware of recent volume and we also need to watch for it during the session ahead. All trading days have heavy volume during the �rst and last hour of the day and lighter volume during the middle of the day. We have to adjust for this so that we can gauge volume on a relative basis. I use a study that calculates the 20-day average volume for every �ve minute increment and that same exact period is referenced so that we are comparing “apples with apples”. I also use a study called relative volume (RVol). It compares the current day’s total volume to the 20-day average volume for the elapsed time. If we are 45 minutes into the trading session, this study compares the cumulative volume today to the 20-day average volume for the �rst 45 minutes of trading. Knowing the market context means that you are aware of your surrounding conditions. Longer-term in�uences and scheduled events are taken into consideration along with important price levels and recent price action. These variables are known to us. Incorporate them into your trading game plan and conduct scenario analysis. Which scenarios are most likely to play out? Which ones present us with the greatest pro�t potential? This framework will provide you with clarity. As the day unfolds, you will understand how this puzzle piece �ts into the big picture and you will be ready to execute your game plan. Moves that previously seemed random will all of a sudden make sense because you are expecting them. Triple witching happens four times a year and we can expect at least one big move during the week.

--- Page 1 ---
Customize appearance Trading Overnight Gaps | OneOption - Stocks & Options Trading Suite Most trading sessions start with an overnight gap. Some are real and some are fake. News releases and overseas markets impact the open. Some days the gap is small and some days the gap is huge. Sometimes the gap is real and sometimes it is fake. For day trading, our opportunities set up in the �rst half of the day. To get your bearings as early as possible you need to start your technical analysis before the open. The long term market trend is currently down (2022 D1 basis) so I will write in those terms because it is easier for me to �nd charts for annotation. The same concepts would apply in reverse if the market was in a long term up trend. Trading gaps can be a little confusing so let’s start with some terms. When I consider a gap up to be “big”, it has to either open above the prior day’s high or it has to be a 1% move above the close from the prior day. If I consider a gap down to be “big”, it has to open below the prior day’s low or it has to be a 1% drop below the prior close. Any other gap is a small gap. If the market is in a long-term down trend, a gap up is considered to be “contra” because it is going against the longer term trend and a gap down is considered to “agree” because it is aligned with the longer term trend. If the longer term trend is up, a gap down would be “contra” because it is going against the longer term trend and a gap up would “agree”. If a gap up has follow through we consider it to be a “Gap and Go”. It is “going” in the direction of the gap. If a gap up collapses, it is called a “Gap Reversal”. If a gap down has follow through we consider it to be a “Gap and Go” because it is “going” in the direction of the gap. If the market gaps down and then bounces, we call it a “Gap Reversal”. The “big” and “small” de�nitions and the “agree” and “contra” designations are not industry standards. I assigned them so that the scenarios are easier to describe and concepts are easier to understand. Big Gap and Go – Agree In a bear market, this would be a big gap down and at very least, the high from the gap down day needs to be lower than the low from the prior day (the gap takes out the prior low) or the drop has to be greater than 1% from the prior close. Some gaps are real and they continue in the direction of the gap. This is called a “Gap and Go”. We can expect these when the gap “agrees” with the longer term trend. The market is currently in a long term down trend so we will use this bear market when we reference the trend. If the gap down is large relative to recent gaps, joining the move presents lower risk once the downward movement is con�rmed . You are joining the longer term trend so the likelihood of a gap reversal is lower compared to the risk of a gap reversal when you are buying a gap up in a bear market (important concept, give this some thought). Shorting large gaps on the open is risky since the gap might be over-extended (fell too far) and some of it could �ll right away. Shorts who aggressively short the open risk getting �ushed out on bounces. We need to watch the price action to con�rm that it is a “Gap and Go” and we do not want to fall victim to a gap reversal (example below in gap reversal section). When the market continues to drop we have technical con�rmation and this becomes a high probability short where you can trade larger size. The key is to watch for consecutive red candles and orderly price movement without much retracement on heavy volume. The bounces (if any) should be brief (no more than 30 minutes) and shallow (the open from long red candles remain intact). Because of the big initial drop, most of the drop has already been realized. These large moves lower last about 90 minutes from the open and then the price action compresses. There could be follow through selling later in the day, but the “lion’s share” of the move has already happened. Don’t fret that you missed a good chunk of the move. You needed that technical con�rmation before you enter and there is plenty of “meat on the bone”. You can trade larger size at this stage of the move and that will offset some of the price drop you missed. You can also ride these trades longer because the threat of any bounce does not come until very late in the day (last 30 minutes typically). Big Gap and Go – Contra In a bear market, this would be a big gap up where at minimum the low from the gap day is higher than the prior day’s high (gap takes out the prior high) or the move up is more than 1% above the prior close. The market does not go straight down or straight up and news typically causes these large gaps that are contrary to the longer-term trend. As of this writing we are in a bear market (2022). In�ation is running wild and the Fed is hiking rates so fast that they might push the economy into a recession. A large gap up could happen because in�ation is starting to ease or from “dovish” Fed statements. The reason for the contra gap does not really matter, the end result is a big gap up that is likely to spark short covering. When we have a big “Gap and Go” against the longer term trend we have to use extra caution. The risk of having the rug pulled out (Gap Reversal) is very high so you do NOT want to buy the open. I have an example of this in the “Gap Reversal” section below. We need to wait for technical con�rmation before we take a position. The market is in a longer term down trend so we know that the selling pressure has been heavy. Stacked long green candles consecutively with little to no overlap early in the session on heavy volume will tell us the rally is real. The open on a “Gap and Go” is often the low of the day and the market shoots higher in the �rst 30 minutes of trading. This is a low reward trade because much of the move will be exhausted by the time we have the technical con�rmation we need. When we get these contra formations I trade smaller size and I wait for a pullback later in the day (happens very often). At some point, pro�t taking will set in. Day traders will be anxious to take gains on longs when they are trading against the longer-term down trend. Longer-term sellers will test the bid (sell orders) when they see resistance forming. If they sense that the bid is fairly strong they will hold off on additional sell orders and they will wait for higher prices. If this dip from the high of the day is relatively small I will look for a day trade on the long side. I want to preserve half of the range between the high today and the open today (not the high today and the prior day’s close) and ideally we stay tight to the high of the day and preserve even more of it. That small retracement tells me that the selling pressure is not organized (no consecutive long red candles) and that for the time being, buyers have control. On any drop, if the bid crumbles and the selling gets organized (nice sized consecutive red candles on volume), we could have a gap reversal setting up. I will discuss this in greater detail later. Just know that in order to trade from the long side on a “Gap and Go Contra”, we have to stay tight to the high of the day. Since I am waiting for a dip later in the day, most of the move has been exhausted. I am also trading smaller size because this is contra to the long term trend. This is not a fantastic trading set up for the reasons I’ve noted, but don’t despair. As you can see in the chart below, they don’t happen often and they typically set up great entry points for shorts where we can join the longer-term down trend. Small Gap and Go – Agree In the context of a bear market, this is a small gap down. These moves agree with the longer term trend and they present a different set of issues and opportunities. The magnitude of the gap is a sign that sellers are not overly aggressive. These gaps can often �ll so we need to make sure that sellers are in control. Our best case scenario is a wimpy bounce into the gap with mixed overlapping candles on light volume. That gives us time to evaluate the price action and to �nd stocks with relative weakness. Ideally, more than half of the gap is preserved. When the bounce stalls we have an excellent entry point for short positions. We know there is selling pressure and we are joining the longer term down trend. Once we have a new low for the day on decent volume, we can short. The market needs to work its way below the prior day’s low and ideally it breaches that support with ease. This is a lower risk trade because we are joining the long term down trend. The potential reward is higher (especially if a D1 support has been breached) because the opening gap was not big. We have plenty of pro�t potential because the opening move is not over-extended. This back drop sets up nice orderly trading and a steady drift lower. There are times when a small gap down will start with consecutive stacked red candles with little to no overlap on decent volume. This is an excellent set up because it indicates heavy selling and the odds of a bear trend day are high. If you see these stacked red candles in the �rst 30 minutes of trading you need to get some shorts on. This is a “short stupid” moment. If chasing makes you nervous (and it should), start scaling in and add on weakness. Because the initial gap down was not that big, you have lots of pro�t potential and a room for the momentum to build and that is why this pattern is better than a Big “Gap and Go Agree”. Watch for stacked red candles an an easy breach of the prior day’s low (sign of heavy selling pressure). Decent volume on the drop will serve as added con�rmation. Small Gap and Go – Contra In this pattern we have a small gap higher in a longer term bearish market. We often see these when the previous day had heavy selling and when the market closed on the low of the day. This little gap is an overnight relief rally from over-extended selling. Often the overnight bounce is instantly squashed when sellers return (“Small Gap Reversal Contra”) so don’t assume that a “Gap and Go” is going to happen. First of all we want to preserve half of the gap (Open minus prior day’s close). That would tell us that buyers are engaged and that they are willing to defend the gap. Stacked consecutive green candles on heavy volume would be the ideal scenario. That would tell us that buyers are aggressive and because the gap up is relatively small we have lots of room to run and a chance for momentum to build. This would set up a major short squeeze. Next we want to attack the prior day’s high and we need to get through that �rst resistance level. Often, the gap up holds and it gradually gains momentum. The move higher will start and stop and sellers are always testing the bid. Remember, this is in the context of a bear market. In the chart below there were not any large pullbacks. This is a sign that buyers are engaged and they will get more aggressive as the day wears on. Shorts will get nervous and they will cover positions. That will create additional buying pressure. This is not a great trading set up because the threat of a “reversal” looms so I trade smaller size. We are trading against the longer term down trend so the price action is going to be jerky. Buyers are constantly looking over their shoulders and the rug could get pulled out at any time. Set passive targets and take gains along the way. Big Gap Reversal – Agree In this pattern the gap down is big and it agrees with the longer-term down trend. Bearish speculators get very excited when they see this and those who have very little patience will short the open. To their surprise, the market reverses and they get the door slammed in their face. This is why we do NOT predict that this is going to be a “Big Gap and Go – Agree”. We have to wait for technical con�rmation that sellers are in control. If the opening low holds immediately and the market moves right into the gap, a reversal is possible. The news that caused the gap might not have been that dire. Trading volume in the overnight session is light and buyers simply pulled their bids and waited for the open. This could have caused an over-reaction/air-pocket. When buyers saw the drop, they did not hesitate. The key for a reversal like this is long green candles and heavy volume. We have to see early signs that buyers are interested. Because there was overnight news and because the longer term trend is down, we are going to see overlapping candles on the bounce. We are also likely to see green candles retrace and there will be and dips. These bounces are hard to trade because you are always looking over your shoulder wondering, “Where did all of the sellers go?” The choppy grind higher is also frustrating because the market spends an hour moving higher and those gains can be wiped out in a couple of bars. Watch for a low in the �rst 30 minutes of trading and a long green candle off of that low. The open of that green candle needs to be preserved. From that point on you want to see a series of higher lows during the day and you want to reach the halfway point of the gap (previous close – today’s open) in the �rst half of the day. The rally needs to happen on heavy volume. If you have these elements, the reversal has a good chance of happening. At some point the downside is going to be tested. That dip should preserve most of the gains from the low and you want to see a higher low. The temptation for day traders will be to short this dip. They want to join the longer term down trend. They saw the big overnight drop and they are looking for a good entry point for shorts. When the market �nds support well above the low it will embolden buyers and they will be active. Shorts will get squeezed and when they cover the next leg higher will unfold. When the gap looks like it has a chance to �ll, sellers will cancel offers on the notion that they will be able to sell at a higher price. That also fuels the move. It is more common to see a down gap reversal off of a relative low (60-day low) than it is off of a relative high. At the low end of the range, the market is typically oversold. Buyers feel like there is value at that price level and bears are eager to take gains on short positions. That is what causes these “reversals”. Big Gap Reversal – Contra In this pattern the big gap up goes against the longer term down trend (contra). These happen when there is big news and there has to be a “surprise” component that catches the market off guard. Are institutions going to support the move or fade it? In the chart below a favorable CPI just before an FOMC statement excited buyers. In�ation had been forcing the Fed to tighten and this “better than feared” in�ation number had the potential to prompt the Fed to take their foot off of the brake. That was the rationale behind the spike and it really does not matter what caused the spike. I just thought this information would add some “color”. We just had to watch the price action. The �rst candle of the day was red and the next few candles could not get back to the opening price (the high of the day). The high touched the 1-year downward sloping trendline. In the �rst 30 minutes of trading we had a new low of the day and the SPY was not close to getting back to the high of the day. The red candles were starting to mount and the volume was extremely heavy. At this stage, a “Big Gap Reversal – Contra” looked likely. It is unusual to see a monster gap up like this fail, but remember we are in a bear market. A move of this magnitude would certainly attract long-term short sellers and shorter-term bulls would be tempted to take pro�ts on longs. If the move held the opening price (bullish), shorts would be running for cover and longer term Asset Managers would start “believing” (buying). Sellers had control and they got more con�dent when the 200-day MA was tested and it failed. “Big Gap Reversal – Contra” set-ups have incredible pro�t potential once there is technical con�rmation. Watch for a high of the day in the �rst few bars, long red candles with heavy volume and a series of new lows. Once the high of the day is in, we do not want any long green candles that test it. Since the reversal joins the longer term down trend our odds of success are relatively high and we can trade larger size. These trades have lots of room to drop and the momentum builds during the day. If there are key technical levels that fail on the way down, the selling pressure will build. Once half of the gap �lls, buyers pull bids and the drop accelerates. These are fantastic trend days so you want to ride your day trading shorts as long as possible. We tend to see this pattern at the extremes of a range. That is where buyers and sellers are most active. If this gap reversal is at a relative high, we can expect follow through selling pressure the next week. This is a clear sign of resistance and it will not go unnoticed. Small Gap Reversal – Agree In the context of a longer-term down trend, the market has a small gap down that agrees with the longer term trend. This seems like a good set-up on the open and it could turn into a “Small Gap and Go – Agree”, but we have to wait. As the price action unfolds, the market �nds support and the gap is reversed. Because the gap down was relatively small, sellers are not that aggressive. The �rst six bars will tell us if this gap is going to “reverse” or “go”. Consecutive green candles are a sign that the gap could easily reverse. This is particularly true if the mid- point of the gap (prior close – open today) is reached or if the low from the prior day is reached. Nice volume with long green candles would suggest that the gap will easily �ll. Often, the candles will be mixed and institutions will try both sides to see if they can get something going. There are times when the market will probe a little deeper after the open, but the candles are mixed and overlapping indicating a weak move lower. There are also times when that probe deeper has tiny bodied candles. This is also a sign of support. The longer the market sits near the opening price, the more likely it is to bounce. Buyers have defended the low and a “Gap and Go” (lower) has been avoided. The scenario in the chart below is not ideal because the gap did not take out the prior day’s low. It did test it and when it did so two bullish hammers were a sign of support. The long green candle off of the low �lled the gap and it was a sign of strength. During the prior 5 trading sessions the S&P 500 had lost 10%. The long green candles and off- setting long red candles came on heavy volume. Buyers and sellers were going to battle it out and we had to expect volatile conditions. The retracement (dip) was big, but the market did �nd support above the low of the day (higher low) and it �nished well off of the low. At very least, short-term support was forming. The selling pressure had been heavy and this little gap down looked like it could gain traction, but it didn’t. It is critically important to patiently wait for the action to unfold. The backdrop looked much different after an hour of trading than it did on the open. Small Gap Reversal – Contra In this pattern we have a small gap up against the longer term down trend hence the designation “contra”. This pattern is common when the selling pressure has been heavy the previous day. Often buyers will test the waters to see if the previous move was over-extended. This little bounce gives us a chance to gauge the selling pressure. Ideally the gap up continues a little higher with mixed overlapping candles and light volume, but we don’t want the move to last more than 30 minutes. The longer it lasts and the higher it goes, the greater the buying pressure. We want that bounce to stall with tiny bodied candles or a bearish engulf or a bearish hammer at the high of the day. That will tell us that sellers have returned and we can prepare to short. If the opening gap higher has consecutive red candles and more than half of the gap is �lled, a gap reversal is likely. Red candles and heavy volume are the keys to �lling the gap and we want to see them in the �rst hour of trading. If the open has been preserved during the �rst hour of trading, a gap reversal is unlikely. That is a sign that buyers are engaged. When you see an overnight gap, here are the questions you need to address: Is the market in a long-term uptrend? The trend is our friend and we always want to join it. A gap up will move in the direction of the trend, but we can’t assume that it is going to be a “Gap and Go”. We like the fact that buyers are engaged and our best case scenario is a small retracement into the gap that �nds instant support. That buys us time to evaluate the price action. Stacked consecutive green candles on the open will force us to take action earlier and much of the move will be exhausted by the time we enter. An overnight gap lower is better in a bull market since we have the chance for a “gap reversal’ with lots of upside potential and a chance for a bullish trend day where we can join the longer-term up trend. Is the market in a long-term downtrend? If it is, a gap up is a day trader’s friend. That bounce will help us gauge the selling pressure and it could lead to an excellent entry point for shorts if a “reversal” forms. We have to watch for signs of early resistance (bearish hammers, bearish engul�ng candle) and we want to start �lling some of the gap in the �rst hour of trading. If the overnight gap is down, we need to con�rm the selling pressure. Long red candles to start the day would indicate a down “Gap and Go” and we might have to “short stupid”. This forces us to take action early in the day and to chase. Did the gap take out the prior day’s range? For big gaps, that is the minimum requirement. A big gap up needs to trade above the prior day’s high and a big gap down needs to trade below the prior day’s low. What was the prior day’s range? If the market was in a tight trading range, eclipsing the high (or the low) is not that di�cult. The prior day’s high and low are relevant because that is resistance and support respectively. If the market had a big range the previous day and it closed on its low, a gap up is not likely to take out the prior day’s high. If it does, it had to travel far to do that and it is signi�cant. When the previous day had a huge range and the gap (up or down) is in that range, it is less signi�cant because this is likely to be an “inside day”. Is the gap going to violate a major moving average? Before the open, we know the indication of where the market is likely to start the day. Is that level going to violate any major D1 moving averages? Is it going to be close to any of them? This is critical information. For instance, if the S&P 500 is in a long-term down trend and it closed above the 100-day MA, a gap down to it the next day is important. If that support fails, the selling pressure will mount and we could see a bearish trend day. You need to know where that support level is and you need to monitor it during the trading day. Is the gap up going to challenge a major down trendline? Evaluate how close the gap up will be to that trendline and plan around it. That could either spark a breakout and we could have a “Gap and Go” with stacked green candles, or we could have a “Gap Reversal” when resistance at the down trendline is con�rmed. In this instance, we had a gap reversal. You were aware of that key price level and you planned for this scenario. Is the gap down going to breach or touch a major up trendline? If it is, you can plan for either scenario. A bounce off of that upward sloping trendline could set up a “Gap Reversal” and we know to watch for stacked green candles that easily move to the middle of the gap early in the day. If the up trendline fails, we know we could have a “Gap and Go” to the downside that results in a bearish trend day. That would tell us that we can ride our short positions because the longer-term market trend is down. In the chart below the market had just closed below the 200-day MA the day before. Follow through selling would send it through the upward sloping trendline and we could see a “Gap and Go” bearish trend day. That scenario seemed very likely and we could plan for it. What has the recent price action been like? Does the gap agree or disagree with the trend? The strength of the trend is going to increase the chances of a “Gap and Go” or a “Gap Reversal”. Is the market trapped in a range with tiny candles and light volume? In the chart below I have highlighted a period like this. These gaps were happening inside of a horizontal compression and they had little meaning. Most of those days the market did not move much. We know that from the tiny bodied candles and the wicks and tails. Did the gap happen near a relative high or a relative low? We know those areas will attract buyers and sellers and the moves can be large. At relative highs we can see up gap “reversals” and they are a sign of resistance. We can expect follow through selling when we see long red candles at a relative high and we can expect some bearish “Gap and Go’s” after that. I highlighted some of those in the chart below. At relative lows we can see down gap “reversals” that indicate support and we can expect the bounce to continue with some “Gap and Go” rallies. Are we seeing long mixed candles on the daily chart with good volume? This is a sign of volatility and we can expect big moves in both directions. That means the gaps could “go” or “reverse”. We need to use caution and we need to con�rm which pattern is forming. What is the status of 1OP on the open? I will discuss day trading with 1OP in greater detail in another section, but it helps us gauge the buying and selling pressure early in the day. If we have a gap down and 1OP is in a bullish cycle, we should see if the market bounces during that bullish cycle and if it �lls in some of the gap. If it does not, we know the selling pressure is heavy and that the bearish cross will set up a great entry for a likely “Gap and Go”. If 1OP is in a bearish cycle and we get a massive gap up, we should watch for selling. If we see stacked red candles during the bear cycle we know that the chances of a “Gap Reversal” are high. I’ve highlighted charts with each of these scenarios below. How big is the gap and why is that important? Big gaps up open well above the prior day’s high and big gaps down open below the prior day’s low. These are the �rst resistance/support levels that the market has to get through each day and if it can’t do that, the gap is less signi�cant. A gap of more than 1% would also qualify as a big gap. A move of this magnitude will often reach other longer-term technical levels. What happens at those levels determines the direction and once we have technical con�rmation, our odds of success improve dramatically. Smaller gaps to a technical support/resistance level can turn into trend days. This happens when there has been a recent trend to that level. Because the gap is relatively small, it can gain momentum when that level is breached and that leads to a trend day with nice consistent price action (because the gap was small the move is not over-extended). If the gap is small and it can’t get through the prior day’s range, it is of little signi�cance and it is likely to reverse. Was the market able to recover half of the gap? When we measure the gap we use the previous closing price and the opening price today. If more than half of the gap is recovered, the chances of a “Gap Reversal” are much higher. It is a sign that the initial move was an over-reaction. If the mid-point is preserved, the chances of a “Gap and Go” increase. Was the opening price the high/low of the day? If the market gaps up and the opening price is the low of the day, we often see stacked green candles and we know that a “Gap and Go” is likely. If the market gaps up and the opening price was the high of the day, we often start with stacked long red candles and the odds of a “Gap Reversal” increase. What is the price action like in the �rst 30 minutes? A wimpy attempt to �ll the gap has mixed overlapping candles on light volume. If more than half of the gap is preserved, this move is likely to fail and the market will move in the direction of the gap. This could quickly turn into a “Gap and Go” and that small move gave us valuable time to gauge the price action and to enter at a good price. We were able to con�rm that the initial direction of the gap was correct. Which scenario is going to play out? Is this going to be a “Gap and Go” or a “Gap Reversal”? What is the best scenario? What is the most likely scenario? How will I trade it? What signs should I look for? I’ve already covered much of this , but it always helps to have fresh examples. Scenario analysis is a process that you should go through before each open. Know the context and visualize what might happen. Plan your actions around these outcomes so that you are ready to execute. It is important for you to conduct scenario analysis before the open each day so that you can be proactive instead of reactive. Gaps are complicated and signi�cant. They are �lled with traps and opportunities. I highlighted 8 different set-ups in the context of a long term market downtrend. Know that there are 8 different set-ups for a long term up trend. The concepts are the same. The “Big Gap and Go Agrees” with the long term trend. By the time we have technical con�rmation much of the move has happened. Here is a video that features a bullish Gap and Go. Big “Gap and Go’s” that agree are more common than Big “Gap and Go Contra’s”, but they are still fairly rare. We can expect follow through selling Big contra “Gap and Go’s” are fairly rare. News sparks short covering in a bear market these moves often retrace a few days later. Once we have technical con�rmation of the Gap and Go we have lots of pro�t potential because the initial gap was small. The move up is tenuous because the long term trend is down and sellers are never far away. Wait for the action to unfold. The price action will tell us if this move is going to “go” or “reverse” and we need that information. Know where the major MAs are and if they might come into play given the overnight gap. When you know where these key price levels are you see if the gap will put them in “play” and you can plan around them. Knowing that a trendline came into play helped us plan our trading day. Gaps that do not touch major price levels or that are inside of a recent range are less important. 1OP was in a bullish cycle during the down gap. When it failed to produce our chances for a “Gap and Go” on the bearish cross increased. We don’t know if the gap is going to “go” or “reverse”. The 1OP indicator helps us gauge which scenario is likely to play out.

--- Page 1 ---
Customize appearance Day Trading Patterns To Watch For | OneOption - Stocks & Options Trading Suite Market First 16 min read 2024-10-28 These patterns are important for long-term and short-term trading, but we lean heavily on them when we Day Trade. Before we get started, please make sure that you’ve read the �rst article on groups of candles in the long-term technical analysis section. The beauty of learning how to read price action is that the same concepts can be applied to any time frame. Here are some patterns that we use frequently for day trading and short-term swing trading. Overlap When we are gauging trend strength, one of the �rst things we notice is overlapping candles. If the current candle moves into the previous candle it has overlap. To be clear, tiny bodied candles don’t have overlap, they are typically retraced completely. The focus for this section is on candles that have some decent length relative to other candles. We have two examples below so let’s focus on the bullish side knowing that the same principles apply to bearish moves. If we have a long green candle, it is a sign that buyers are aggressive. They were able to lift the “ask” and that resulted in a longer than average candle. The ultimate scenario is that the volume is heavy and the current candle low is the high from the previous candle. That is what we call “stacked” and it is a sign of aggressive buying especially if we can stack a few of them consecutively. We don’t see that often, but when we do, we expect follow through buying. Most candles will have some retracement. The next best case for continuation would be a current candle that dips into the previous candle, but the half-way point is preserved. Buyers want to buy any dip and they layer bids at a lower prices. Sellers recognize the strength (they hit bids and the bids are replenished instantly) so they hold off on additional sell orders because they expect higher prices. The current candle �nishes higher than the open and it �nishes above the high from the previous candle. The outcome is a nice green candle with a tail. That move higher should continue and this is a moderately strong pattern, but it is not as strong as a stacked candle. A less desirable combination for bullish traders is a current candle that retraces the entire previous candle and that can’t get through the high from the previous candle. It does �nish close to the previous candle close and it could have a small red body or a small green body. This level of retracement tells us that sellers had the power to “clear” those bids. Buyers did return, but not with a vengeance. If this rally continues with similar candles, the move higher will be very tenuous and eventually the trend is vulnerable to a reversal. If the current candle closes below the mid-point of the previous long green candle and it has a wick, we are getting close to resistance. Buyers tried to advance the stock and sellers overpowered them. In the chart below, the pattern on the left is fairly decent. This move should have more upside. The candles are overlapping, but they are green and they are �nishing above the previous high. The pattern on the right is weaker. We can see that the current candle is retracing the entire previous candle and they are closing below the prior high. This move higher is vulnerable to pro�t taking and it is getting exhausted. Wicks and Tails The area above the body of the candle is called the wick and the area below the body is called the tail. If the body of the candle comprises less than half of the range, the tails and wicks are considered to be long. If the body �nishes in the middle of the range, it is a sign of indecision. Long wicks and tails are your clue. They are telling you that the stock �nished well off of its high and well off of its low. When we see these candles in the middle of a trend, it is a sign that at very least, a pause is coming. The trend could continue, but it might take time to digest the recent move. When the body of the candle is less than a quarter of the range and the range is normal, I consider this to be a doji. The classic de�nition is that the close is equal to the open for a doji. I am less interested in perfect conformity to a de�nition and I am more focused on what the candle is telling me. Buyer and sellers have both taken a shot and they moved the stock around. The open and the close were near each other and neither side was able to move the needle. This is a sign of indecision. As traders, we should expect a move one way or the other and we need to wait for it. When we see mixed candles with long tails and wicks, it is a sign that a compression is likely, particularly if this happens on light volume. Neither side has control and you should reduce your trade count and trade size. When the wick or the tail is long and the body is at the high or the low of the range we have a “hammer”. Let’s cover that next. Hammers Hammers are candles that have a nice range and they either have a long wick or a long tail. The body is small by comparison and it is concentrated on one end of the range. If the wick is long and the body is at the low end of the range, it is a bearish hammer. By de�nition, the close should be lower than the open, but that is not that important to me. I prefer red bearish hammers, but the message is the same. The stock tried to rally and sellers drove the price down. If the tail is long and the body is at the high end of the range, it is a bullish hammer. By de�nition, the close of the candle should be higher than the open. I prefer green bullish hammers, but the price action tells me that buyers are engaged. Buyers drove the stock to the upper end of the range. In the chart below we see a bearish hammer on the left side of the chart. This candlestick pattern is very important at a relative high. It is a sign of stiff resistance. Notice the two long green candles before it. At one time, the bearish hammer was a third stacked “green”. Buyers were excited and they expected lift-off. When the candle completed, the complexion changed dramatically. Tip: This is why we do not assume that a candle will �nish strong or weak, we wait for it. Often it will change at the last second. Sellers imposed their will and they smashed bids. Soon FOMO buyers who rushed in to buy that third stacked “green” that was forming will regret that trade. When they bail it will add to the selling pressure. Would you have avoided this trap? I hope so, the two stacked “greens” came on light volume and there was overlap. No reason to chase this move, wait for the candle to complete. As sellers take control, we see mixed overlapping candles on low volume. That is a sign that the trend lower is weak. Two nice long red candles are a sign of selling pressure and a third long red candle is forming at the low. When it completes, it turns into a bullish hammer and the trend reverses. See how this works? Some of you are going to read this and think, “Pete doesn’t know shit about candlestick patterns. He doesn’t even know the rules.” I’ve read the books (Nison and Pring are good authors) and constructed searches for these exact patterns. When I looked at the results, I realized that I was missing some of the best trades because they did not �t the de�nition perfectly. That’s when I started to focus more on what the price action was telling me and less on the de�nition. Don’t memorize de�nitions, learn the message and then you won’t need to know about “abandon babies” and “evening stars” and three dogs barking (made that one up). Engul�ng Candles When I think of engul�ng candles, I think of the �rst video game I played called Pac-Man. The current candle consumes the entire previous candle. By de�nition, the current candle needs to open above the prior high and it needs to close below the prior low to qualify as a bearish engul�ng candle. Think about this. Most candles have a wick. On an intraday chart, the stock for some reason has to gap up above the high on the next M5 bar and then it has to tank and close below the prior low. You might see this on a D1 chart because we have overnight gaps, but you are very rarely going to see this intraday. So here is what I want for my bearish engul�ng candles. If the previous candle had a long wick, cool. Sellers are lined up. I want the open of the current candle to be roughly equal to the previous close. Buyers are still interested, but that enthusiasm is about to get squashed. Sellers smash the bid and they drive the stock down. This is the important part for my de�nition. I want to obliterate the previous low and I want to close well below it. I want a nice long red candle and a tiny tail. That price action tells me that sellers are in complete control and buyers were powerless (candle closes near the low). When we get this pattern near a relative high, it is a sign that a short-term high is forming. This could also be the start of a trend reversal. In the chart below, you can see this pattern on the left side of the chart. Mixed overlapping green candles are a sign of weak trend strength and this bearish engul�ng candle con�rms it. The down trend features some nice long red candles and then we have a bullish hammer (by my de�nition) at the low. The classic de�nition is that the open of the bullish engul�ng candle is lower than the low of the previous candle and the close of the bullish engul�ng candle is higher than the high from the previous candle. Again, you might see this on a daily chart because of overnight gaps, but you will not see this intraday. I want the low of the current candle to be close to the low of the previous candle. In this case, the long tail of the previous candle is welcome and I don’t care that we are not close to it. Buyers are already lined up. The open of the engul�ng candle is roughly equal to the close of the previous candle. Now for the part that really matters. I want buyers to lift every “ask” in sight and to leave sellers powerless. That will yield the long bodied green candle. I want that close substantially above the high from the prior candle and I want that wick to be tiny. That is a sign of support and aggressive buying. At very least, we can expect a bounce and that will be a short- term low. It could lead to a trend reversal and this pattern is most potent near a relative low. Retracements Stocks do not go straight up or straight down. We should expect pauses and “�ts and spurts” along the way. The frequency, duration and magnitude of these retracements help us gauge trend strength. In the chart below we can see that the trend is relatively weak. There are mixed overlapping candles with tiny bodies and the volume is light. We can trade this trend, but we have to be very careful. The rug can get pulled out at any time. Ride the momentum and watch for any sign of trouble. In this case, you can see the bearish engul�ng candle after the new high. This is a sign for you to take pro�ts on long positions and it might be time to line up some shorts. The market tries to recover, but it can’t get anywhere close to the previous high. These are signs that the weak trend has run out of gas. After a couple of consecutive red candles with heavy volume and a trendline breach, we can be con�dent a reversal is coming. This is a major retracement and 3 hours worth of bullish price action are erased in 15 minutes. Notice how that heavy selling pressure into the close spilled over to the next day and we had a big overnight gap down. Try to visualize a pattern that I am going to describe to you. There is a trend down with overlapping candles and each bounce retraces more than half of the recent move. That pattern repeats so there are lower highs and lower lows. These are major retracements so the trend lower is weak. In your mind connect the highs and connect the lows. Can you visualize the pattern? If you guessed a downward sloping channel, you are correct. When the trend is strong, the retracements should be brief and shallow. Let’s use a bearish example since I have a chart ready. The same concept applies to bullish trends. I like pauses and bounces during the drop to last less than 30 minutes. If they last longer than that, it is a sign of support. If the pause lasts less than 30 minutes it is a sign that sellers are aggressive. We measure moves from the last bounce or pause to the next bounce or pause. **Candle-by-candle observation (right chart):**
- The sequence starts with green candles at the top, then shifts to mixed and red candles moving down.
- A cluster of small-bodied candles appears as the decline slows.

- After this overlap event, the chart shows some green candles emerging, suggesting a potential reversal.

## 3. PATTERN OR CONCEPT BEING TAUGHT

### The "Overlap" Pattern

This chart teaches the **Overlap** pattern — a reversal signal that occurs when a candle's price action retraces or overlaps back into (or through) the prior candle's range after what appeared to be a continuation of the trend.

**Two variations are shown:**

**Variation 1 (D1 — Gap Down, Close Higher):**
- **Rule:** "When price gaps down below the prior candle in a downtrend BUT then closes higher than the prior candle's close (or back into its body range), this is an overlap signal indicating potential bullish reversal."
- The gap down initially suggests continuation of selling pressure, but the fact that buyers pushed the price all the way back up to close higher signals that sellers have lost control and demand is stepping in.

**Variation 2 (M5 — Tail Completely Retraces Prior Candle):**
- **Rule:** "When a candle's tail/wick extends below the prior candle's range but then completely retraces back up through the prior candle, this is an overlap signal indicating potential bullish reversal."
- The long lower tail shows that sellers initially pushed price lower, but aggressive buying absorbed all the selling and drove price back above the prior candle's range — a powerful rejection of lower prices.

**General Rule for Overlap:**
> "When a candle in a downtrend initially extends the move lower (via gap or wick) but then reverses to close back into or above the prior candle's range, this 'overlap' signals a potential trend reversal. Traders should watch for this as a sign that the prevailing trend is losing momentum."

**What a trader should look for:**
- A clear established downtrend preceding the pattern
- A candle that initially extends the downtrend (gaps down or wicks down significantly)
- That same candle then reversing to close back into or through the prior candle's territory
- Confirmation via subsequent bullish candles following the overlap

**What a trader should avoid:**
- Trading the overlap in isolation without a preceding trend
- Ignoring the context — the pattern is meaningful specifically because it occurs after a sustained move
- Confusing normal retracement candles with true overlap signals (the key is the dramatic reversal within a single candle)

---

## 4. MY UNDERSTANDING — CORE INSIGHT

The deep insight here is about **failed continuation as a reversal signal**. The Overlap pattern is powerful precisely because of the psychological and order-flow dynamics it represents:

### Why This Pattern Matters

The overlap is essentially a **trap and reversal**. In a downtrend, when price gaps down or extends lower via a long wick, it initially attracts more short sellers who believe the trend is continuing. These late shorts are entering at the worst possible moment. When price then reverses violently and closes back above the prior candle's range, all of those late shorts are now **trapped in losing positions**. Their stop-losses (placed above recent candles) will fuel the buying pressure as the reversal unfolds.

### The Two Timeframe Examples Are Intentional

By showing D1 and M5 side by side, the author is demonstrating that this is a **fractal concept** — it works across all timeframes. A day trader watching 5-minute charts can apply the exact same logic as a swing trader on daily charts. The underlying market psychology (failed breakdown → trapped sellers → reversal) is identical regardless of timeframe.

### What Makes It Valid vs. Invalid

**Valid overlap:**
- Occurs after a clear, multi-candle downtrend (not in choppy/range-bound conditions)
- The candle shows clear initial extension of the downtrend (gap or long wick) followed by a dramatic reversal
- The close is meaningfully back into or above the prior candle's range — not just a marginal overlap
- Ideally accompanied by increased volume on the reversal
- Subsequent candles confirm with bullish follow-through

**Invalid/weak overlap:**
- Occurs in a sideways market where candles are already overlapping regularly (no trend context)
- The "overlap" is minimal — just barely retracing into the prior candle without conviction
- The reversal candle has a small body relative to its range, suggesting indecision rather than conviction
- No follow-through in subsequent candles — price stalls or resumes the downtrend

### The Core Takeaway

**The most powerful reversals often begin with what looks like trend continuation.** The overlap pattern captures the exact moment when the market "tries and fails" to continue the trend. The failure itself becomes the catalyst. A seasoned trader internalizes this: *when the market extends in one direction and snaps back aggressively within a single candle, the message is clear — the dominant side has exhausted itself, and the other side is taking control.* This is not just a pattern to memorize; it's a window into the battle between buyers and sellers at a critical inflection point.

This is a **candlestick chart** displaying price action for an unspecified instrument over what appears to be a series of trading sessions (likely daily or intraday candles). The chart shows a general pattern of decline on the left, a bottoming process in the middle, and a recovery/rally on the right side.
